observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -1 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-5{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-(\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2} \\ {R}_{2}:=(\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\  & ={x}_{2}+2(0) \\  & ={x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Find an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -1 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -3\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -1 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-5{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-(\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2} \\ {R}_{2}:=(\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\  & ={x}_{2}+2(0) \\  & ={x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3-\lambda  & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )[(3-\lambda )^{2}-1] & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +8) & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda -4)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=4,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}]-(2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0 \\ -{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{3}.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{3}{1}=3.$

question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$

\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3-\lambda  & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )[(3-\lambda )^{2}-1] & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +8) & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda -4)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}]-(2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0 \\ -{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{3}.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{3}{1}=3.$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -5 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{c}?$
question.worked_solution:
Since $A$ is a lower triangular matrix, we have that its eigenvalues are the entries in the main diagonal, that is, ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ 

Also, since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-5.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=6.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =6.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -5 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-6[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -11 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-5{x}_{1}=0 \\ -3{x}_{1}-11{x}_{2}=0 \\ {x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 0 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -11 & 0 & 0 \\ 1 & 2 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{1}↔{R}_{3} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ -3 & -11 & 0 & 0 \\ -5 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+5{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 10 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+2{R}_{2} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & -5 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}=0.$ From the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=0.$ Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{c}=\frac{0}{1}=0.$

In our case, we have $\lambda =6.$ So, we obtain

$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda  & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 3 \\ 2 & 4-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )((-1-\lambda )(4-\lambda )-(3)(2)) & =0 \\ (1-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -10) & =0 \\ -(\lambda -1)(\lambda +2)(\lambda -5) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=1,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=-2,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=1$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=-2.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=5.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =5.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & 4 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 2 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0 & -4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-6{x}_{1}+3{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 2{x}_{1}-{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0 \\ -4{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 2 & -1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+\frac{1}{3}{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{5}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{12}{5}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-6 & 3 & 2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \frac{5}{3} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

question.name: Question 3
question.problem:
Find an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 3 \\ -9 & 7 & 5 \\ -5 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 3 \\ -9 & 7 & 5 \\ -5 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 \\ -9 & 4 & 5 \\ -5 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-5{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0 \\ -9{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ -9 & 4 & 5 & 0 \\ -5 & 2 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{9}{5}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{2}{5} & -\frac{2}{5} & 0 \\ -5 & 2 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{2}{5} & -\frac{2}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{5}(2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(2{x}_{3}+3{x}_{3}) \\  & ={x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Question 3
?

Find an eigenvector of A=[−223−975−526] that corresponds to the eigenvalue λ=3.

a
[111]
b
[6−30]
c
[5−420]
d
[10−810]
e
[4520]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=3. So, we obtain

A−λI=[−223−975−526]−3[100010001]=[−523−945−523].

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

{−5x1+2x2+3x3=0−9x1+4x2+5x3=0−5x1+2x2+3x3=0

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix M to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[−5230−9450−5230]R2:=R2+(−95)R1∼[−5230025−250−5230]R3:=R3+(−1)R1∼[−5230025−2500000]

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the 1st and the 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain x2=x3. Substituting this in the first equation, we get x1=15(2x2+3x3)=15(2x3+3x3)=x3.

Therefore, the general solution is [x3x3x3],x3∈R.

Setting, for instance, x3=1, we get the eigenvector v=[111].

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 3 \\ -9 & 7 & 5 \\ -5 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 \\ -9 & 4 & 5 \\ -5 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-5{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0 \\ -9{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ -9 & 4 & 5 & 0 \\ -5 & 2 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{9}{5}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{2}{5} & -\frac{2}{5} & 0 \\ -5 & 2 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{2}{5} & -\frac{2}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{5}(2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(2{x}_{3}+3{x}_{3}) \\  & ={x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=3. So, we obtain

A−λI=[−223−975−526]−3[100010001]=[−523−945−523].

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

{−5x1+2x2+3x3=0−9x1+4x2+5x3=0−5x1+2x2+3x3=0

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix M to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[−5230−9450−5230]R2:=R2+(−95)R1∼[−5230025−250−5230]R3:=R3+(−1)R1∼[−5230025−2500000]

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the 1st and the 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain x2=x3. Substituting this in the first equation, we get x1=15(2x2+3x3)=15(2x3+3x3)=x3.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem:
Find an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 3 \\ -9 & 7 & 5 \\ -5 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3.$
feedback.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 & 3 \\ -9 & 7 & 5 \\ -5 & 2 & 6\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 \\ -9 & 4 & 5 \\ -5 & 2 & 3\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-5{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0 \\ -9{x}_{1}+4{x}_{2}+5{x}_{3}=0 \\ -5{x}_{1}+2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ -9 & 4 & 5 & 0 \\ -5 & 2 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-\frac{9}{5}){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{2}{5} & -\frac{2}{5} & 0 \\ -5 & 2 & 3 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}-5 & 2 & 3 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{2}{5} & -\frac{2}{5} & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & =\frac{1}{5}(2{x}_{2}+3{x}_{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(2{x}_{3}+3{x}_{3}) \\  & ={x}_{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Find an eigenvector of $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -1 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -3\end{aligned}]$
that corresponds to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2.$
question.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -1 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-5{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-(\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2} \\ {R}_{2}:=(\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\  & ={x}_{2}+2(0) \\  & ={x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=3. So, we obtain

A−λI=[1123−1−23−3−3]−2[100010001]=[−1123−3−23−3−5].

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

{−x1+x2+2x3=03x1−3x2−2x3=03x1−3x2−5x3=0

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix M to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -1 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-5{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-(\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2} \\ {R}_{2}:=(\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\  & ={x}_{2}+2(0) \\  & ={x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -1 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-5{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-(\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2} \\ {R}_{2}:=(\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\  & ={x}_{2}+2(0) \\  & ={x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector
$v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

feedback.worked_solution:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =3.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -1 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -3\end{aligned}]-2[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 \\ 3 & -3 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-{x}_{1}+{x}_{2}+2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-2{x}_{3}=0 \\ 3{x}_{1}-3{x}_{2}-5{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}:=(-1){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -2 & 0 \\ 3 & -3 & -5 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}-3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-3{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-(\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2} \\ {R}_{2}:=(\frac{1}{4}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 & -2 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $3$rd). Thus, ${x}_{2}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{3}=0.$ Substituting this in the first equation, we get 

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & ={x}_{2}+2{x}_{3} \\  & ={x}_{2}+2(0) \\  & ={x}_{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2} \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{2}=1,$ we get the eigenvector

question.name: Question 5
question.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

The vectors ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4$ of the matrix $A,$ given above. Find the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}=[a,\,b,\,c]^{T}$ such that the set $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\}$ is linearly independent. What is the value of $\frac{a}{b}?$
question.worked_solution:
First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3-\lambda  & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )[(3-\lambda )^{2}-1] & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +8) & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda -4)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=4,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}]-(2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0 \\ -{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{3}.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{3}{1}=3.$

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we find all the eigenvalues of $A$ by solving the characteristic equation $det(A-\lambda I)=0:$

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3-\lambda  & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )|\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & -1 \\ -1 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )[(3-\lambda )^{2}-1] & =0 \\ (3-\lambda )({\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda +8) & =0 \\ (\lambda -3)(\lambda -4)(\lambda -2) & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ ${\lambda }_{2}=4,$ and ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors $\{{v}_{1},{v}_{2},{v}_{3}\},$ where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that ${v}_{1}$ and ${v}_{2}$ correspond to the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=4.$ Thus, the third eigenvector ${v}_{3}$ must correspond to ${\lambda }_{3}=2.$ 

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\lambda =2.$ So, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 3 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 3\end{aligned}]-(2)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}-3{x}_{3}=0 \\ {x}_{2}-{x}_{3}=0 \\ -{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}=0\end{aligned}
$$

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix $M$ to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}M & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{2}+{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -3 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & -1 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the $1$st and the $2$nd). Thus, ${x}_{3}$ is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain ${x}_{2}={x}_{3}.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we get ${x}_{1}=3{x}_{3}.$
Therefore, the general solution is

$$
[\begin{aligned}3{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{3}\in R.
$$

Setting, for instance, ${x}_{3}=1,$ we get the following eigenvector:

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}a \\ b \\ c\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Finally, $\frac{a}{b}=\frac{3}{1}=3.$

Question 5
?

A=[30−303−10−13] The vectors v1 and v2 are eigenvectors that correspond to the eigenvalues λ1=3 and λ2=4 of the matrix A, given above. Find the third eigenvector v3=[a,b,c]T such that the set {v1,v2,v3} is linearly independent. What is the value of ab?

a
 −1
b
 2
c
 −3
d
3
e
 −2
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we find all the eigenvalues of A by solving the characteristic equation det(A−λI)=0:

det(A−λI)=0|3−λ0−303−λ−10−13−λ|=0(3−λ)|3−λ−1−13−λ|=0(3−λ)[(3−λ)2−1]=0(3−λ)(λ2−6λ+8)=0(λ−3)(λ−4)(λ−2)=0

Hence, λ1=3, λ2=4, and λ3=2. Since we obtained three distinct eigenvalues, the set of eigenvectors {v1,v2,v3}, where each vector corresponds to different eigenvalue, will be linearly independent.

Now, recall that v1 and v2 correspond to the eigenvalues λ1=3 and λ2=4. Thus, the third eigenvector v3 must correspond to λ3=2.

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation (A−λI)x=0.

In our case, we have λ=2. So, we obtain

A−λI=[30−303−10−13]−(2)[100010001]=[10−301−10−11].

To find the eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, we have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:

{x1−3x3=0x2−x3=0−x2+x3=0

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix M to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

M=[10−3001−100−110]R3:=R2+R3∼[10−3001−100000].

In the reduced matrix above, there are two pivot columns (the 1st and the 2nd). Thus, x3 is a free variable. From the second equation, we obtain x2=x3. Substituting this into the first equation, we get x1=3x3. Therefore, the general solution is [3x3x3x3],x3∈R.

Setting, for instance, x3=1, we get the following eigenvector:

v=[abc]=[311]

Finally, ab=31=3.

solution.reasoning: The eigenvalues sum to trace(A)=9, so the third eigenvalue is 9−3−4=2. Solving (A−2I)v₃=0 gives a=3c and b=c, with c≠0. Hence a/b=3, option d. No Math Academy answer-key or grading evidence was supplied.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|6x-2|\sqrt{9+(3x-1)^{2}}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|6x-2|\sqrt{9+(3x-1)^{2}}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{6|x-\frac{1}{3}|\sqrt{9+9{(x-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{|x-\frac{1}{3}|\sqrt{1+{(x-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-\frac{1}{3}.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{|x-\frac{1}{3}|\sqrt{1+{(x-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x-\frac{1}{3})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\frac{3x-1}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(6x-4)\sqrt{9-(3x-2)^{2}}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(6x-4)\sqrt{9-(3x-2)^{2}}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{6(x-\frac{2}{3})\sqrt{9-9{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})\sqrt{1-{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-\frac{2}{3}.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})\sqrt{1-{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-\frac{2}{3})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(\frac{3x-2}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{4-(x+3)^{2}}\text{d}x.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{1}{4-(x+3)^{2}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{4-4{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+3}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+3}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x+3}{2}|>1.$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x+1)\sqrt{9-(3x+3)^{2}}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x+1)\sqrt{9-(3x+3)^{2}}} & =\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x+1)\sqrt{9-9{(x+1)}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x+1.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x+1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x-1)\sqrt{4-(2x-2)^{2}}}.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x-1)\sqrt{4-(2x-2)^{2}}} & =\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x-1)\sqrt{4-4{(x-1)}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{1-(x-1)^{2}}}\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x-1.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$

$$

questions.problem: $\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{(x-1)\sqrt{4+2x-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}+2x+4 & =-({x}^{2}-2x-4) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}-4) \\  & =-((x-1)^{2}-5) \\  & =5-(x-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{(x-1)\sqrt{4+2x-{x}^{2}}} & =\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{(x-1)\sqrt{5-{(x-1)}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})\sqrt{5-5{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{(x-1)\sqrt{4+2x-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: $\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{-4{x}^{2}-8x}}\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{x}^{2}-8x & =-4({x}^{2}+2x) \\  & =-4({x}^{2}+2\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}) \\  & =-4[(x+1)^{2}-1] \\  & =4[1-(x+1)^{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{-4{x}^{2}-8x}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{4[1-(x+1)^{2}]}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x+1.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{-4{x}^{2}-8x}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x+1)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-4x-3 & =-({x}^{2}+4x+3) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}+3) \\  & =-((x+2)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x+2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x-3}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{1-(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x+2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x-3}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{1-(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x+2)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}+10x-24 & =-({x}^{2}-10x+24) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 5x+{5}^{2}-{5}^{2}+24) \\  & =-((x-5)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x-5)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(3x-15)\sqrt{10x-{x}^{2}-24}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x-5)\sqrt{1-(x-5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-5.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(3x-15)\sqrt{10x-{x}^{2}-24}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x-5)\sqrt{1-(x-5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-5)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: $\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{4x-{x}^{2}-3}}\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-{x}^{2}-3 & =-({x}^{2}-4x+3) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}+3) \\  & =-((x-2)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{4x-{x}^{2}-3}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{1-(x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{4x-{x}^{2}-3}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{1-(x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-2)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}+6x+10 & =9({x}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{10}{9}) \\  & =9({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{3}x+{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}+\frac{10}{9}) \\  & =9[{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2}+1]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{|3x+1|\sqrt{9{x}^{2}+6x+10}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{3}|\sqrt{9[1+{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2}]}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{3}|\sqrt{1+{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x+\frac{1}{3}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{3}|\sqrt{1+{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x+\frac{1}{3})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+4x+5 & =4({x}^{2}+x+\frac{5}{4}) \\  & =4({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{5}{4}) \\  & =4[{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+1]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{|2x+1|\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+4x+5}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{2}|\sqrt{4[1+{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}]}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x+\frac{1}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x+\frac{1}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6x+13 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}+13 \\  & =(x+3)^{2}+4\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{6}{|x+3|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x+13}}\,\text{d}x & =-\int \frac{6}{|x+3|\sqrt{4+(x+3)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{6}{2|\frac{x+3}{2}|\sqrt{4+4{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+3}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+3}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+3}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =-\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =-3\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\frac{x+3}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+5 & ={x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}+5 \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{2}{|4x-8|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-4x+5}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{2}{4|x-2|\sqrt{1+(x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|x-2|\sqrt{1+(x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|x-2|\sqrt{1+(x-2)^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x-2)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: $\int \frac{4}{|x+1|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+2x+5}}\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x+5 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}+5 \\  & =(x+1)^{2}+4\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4}{|x+1|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+2x+5}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{4}{|x+1|\sqrt{4+(x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{2}{|\frac{x+1}{2}|\sqrt{4+4{(\frac{x+1}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+1}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+1}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+1}{2})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-2\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\frac{x+1}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

∫4|x+1|x2+2x+5dx=

M

questions.name: Question 16
questions.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-4x-{x}^{2} & =-({x}^{2}+4x-1) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}-1) \\  & =-((x+2)^{2}-5) \\  & =5-(x+2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-4x-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{5-(x+2)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2))+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{5}})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{5}}|>1.$

questions.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{9-(x+4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{1}{9-(x+4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{9-9(\frac{1}{9}(x+4)^{2})}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{3}(x+4))}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{3}(x+4).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{3}(x+4))}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{9}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+4}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x+4}{3}|>1.$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x-{x}^{2}-5 & =-({x}^{2}-6x+5) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}+5) \\  & =-((x-3)^{2}-4) \\  & =4-(x-3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{6x-{x}^{2}-5}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{4-(x-3)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{2}(x-3))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{2}(x-3).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{2}(x-3))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{2}(x-3))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x-3}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x-3}{2}|>1.$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}12x-{x}^{2}-33 & =-({x}^{2}-12x+33) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 6x+{6}^{2}-{6}^{2}+33) \\  & =-((x-6)^{2}-3) \\  & =3-(x-6)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{12x-{x}^{2}-33}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{3-(x-6)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6))+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x-6}{\sqrt{3}})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x-6}{\sqrt{3}}|>1.$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}12+4x-{x}^{2} & =-({x}^{2}-4x-12) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}-12) \\  & =-((x-2)^{2}-16) \\  & =16-(x-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{12+4x-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{16-(x-2)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{4}(x-2))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{4}(x-2).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{4}(x-2))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 4\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{4}(x-2))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x-2}{4})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x-2}{4}|>1.$

Example: 
                    Computing an Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Integral Containing a Completed Square
canonical_examples.problem: Calculate $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{4-(2x-2)^2} \textrm{d}x.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{4-(2x-2)^2}\textrm{d}x = 
\int \dfrac{1}{4-4(x-1)^2}\textrm{d}x = 
\dfrac{1}{4} {\int}\dfrac{1}{ 1 - (x-1)^2 }\textrm{d}x.
$$

Let $u = x-1.$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(x-1)}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(x-1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $\left|{x-1} \right| >   1.$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arsecant Integral
canonical_examples.problem: ${\displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{2x-x^2}} \textrm{d}x= }$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\eqalign{
2x-x^2 & = -(x^2 - 2x)\[5pt]
& = -(x^2 - 2\cdot x + 1^2-1^2)\[5pt]
& = -((x-1)^2 - 1) \[5pt]
&= 1 - (x-1)^2
}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{2x-x^2}} \textrm{d}x  = \int  \dfrac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt { 1-(x-1)^2 } }	\, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Let $u = x-1.$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{2x-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{1-(x-1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-1)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcosecant Integral
canonical_examples.problem: ${\displaystyle \int \dfrac{6}{|3x+9|\sqrt{x^2+6x+10}} \textrm{d}x= }$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6x+10 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}+10 \\  & =(x+3)^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \dfrac{6}{|3x\!+\!9|\sqrt{x^2\!+\!6x\!+\!10}} \,\textrm{d}x  = \int  \dfrac{6}{3|x\!+\!3|\sqrt {1\!+\!(x\!+\!3)^2} }	\, \textrm{d}x = {2} \int \dfrac{1}{|x\!+\!3|\sqrt{1\!+\!(x\!+\!3)^2}} \, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Let $u = x+3.$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}2\int \frac{1}{|x+3|\sqrt{1+(x+3)^{2}}}\text{d}x & =2\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-2\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x+3)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral
canonical_examples.problem: $\displaystyle \int \dfrac{1}{3-2x-x^2} \textrm{d}x=$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\eqalign{
3-2x-x^2 & = -(x^2 + 2x - 3)\[5pt]
& = -(x^2 + 2\cdot x +1^2 - 1^2 - 3)\[5pt]
& = -((x+1)^2 - 4) \[5pt]
&= 4 - (x+1)^2
}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{3-2x-x^2}\textrm{d}x =
\int \dfrac{1}{4-(x+1)^2}\textrm{d}x = 
\dfrac{1}{4} {\int}\dfrac{1}{ 1 - \left( \frac{1}{2}(x+1)\right)^2 }\textrm{d}x.
$$

Let $u = \dfrac{1}{2}(x+1).$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = 2\,\textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{2}(x+1))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{2}(x+1))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+1}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $\left|\dfrac {x+1} {2} \right| >   1.$

EXPLANATION

Let u=x−13. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

question.knowledge_point: Computing an Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Integral Containing a Completed Square

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing an Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Integral Containing a Completed Square
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(6x-4)\sqrt{9-(3x-2)^{2}}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{6(x-\frac{2}{3})\sqrt{9-9{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})\sqrt{1-{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-\frac{2}{3}.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})\sqrt{1-{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-\frac{2}{3})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(\frac{3x-2}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(6x-4)\sqrt{9-(3x-2)^{2}}}.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(6x-4)\sqrt{9-(3x-2)^{2}}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{6(x-\frac{2}{3})\sqrt{9-9{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})\sqrt{1-{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-\frac{2}{3}.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})\sqrt{1-{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-\frac{2}{3})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(\frac{3x-2}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.knowledge_point: Computing an Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Integral Containing a Completed Square

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing an Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Integral Containing a Completed Square
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{1}{4-(x+3)^{2}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{4-4{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+3}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+3}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x+3}{2}|>1.$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{4-(x+3)^{2}}\text{d}x.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{1}{4-(x+3)^{2}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{4-4{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+3}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+3}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x+3}{2}|>1.$

Question 3
?

Calculate ∫14−(x+3)2dx.

a
12arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
b
12arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
c
14arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
d
2arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
e
14arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that ∫14−(x+3)2dx=∫14−4(x+32)2dx=14∫11−(x+32)2dx.

Let u=x+32. Then, we have dudx=12⟹dx=2du.

Therefore, 14∫11−(x+32)2dx=14∫11−u2⋅2du=12∫11−u2du=12⋅arcoth⁡u+C=12arcoth⁡(x+32)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x+32|>1.
question.knowledge_point: Computing an Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Integral Containing a Completed Square

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Computing an Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Integral Containing a Completed Square
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x+1)\sqrt{9-(3x+3)^{2}}} & =\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x+1)\sqrt{9-9{(x+1)}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x+1.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x+1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x-1)\sqrt{4-(2x-2)^{2}}} & =\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x-1)\sqrt{4-4{(x-1)}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{1-(x-1)^{2}}}\text{d}x.\end{aligned}

$$

Therefore,

$$

$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\eqalign{
2x-x^2 & = -(x^2 - 2x)\[5pt]
& = -(x^2 - 2\cdot x + 1^2-1^2)\[5pt]
& = -((x-1)^2 - 1) \[5pt]
&= 1 - (x-1)^2
}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{2x-x^2}} \textrm{d}x  = \int  \dfrac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt { 1-(x-1)^2 } }	\, \textrm{d}x.
$$

Let $u = x-1.$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = \textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{2x-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{1-(x-1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-1)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}+2x+4 & =-({x}^{2}-2x-4) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}-4) \\  & =-((x-1)^{2}-5) \\  & =5-(x-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{(x-1)\sqrt{4+2x-{x}^{2}}} & =\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{(x-1)\sqrt{5-{(x-1)}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})\sqrt{5-5{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{(x-1)\sqrt{4+2x-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

∫5(x−1)4+2x−x2dx=

a
−arsech⁡(x−15)+C
b
15arcsch⁡(x−15)+C
c
−15arsech⁡(x−15)+C
d
−5arsech⁡(x−15)+C
e
arcsch⁡(x−15)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: −x2+2x+4=−(x2−2x−4)=−(x2−2⋅x+12−12−4)=−((x−1)2−5)=5−(x−1)2

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫5(x−1)4+2x−x2=∫5(x−1)5−(x−1)2dx=∫1(x−15)5−5(x−15)2dx=15∫1(x−15)1−(x−15)2dx.

Let u=x−15. Then, we have dudx=15⟹dx=5du.

Therefore,

∫5(x−1)4+2x−x2dx=15∫1(x−15)1−(x−15)2dx=15∫1u1−u2⋅5du=∫1u1−u2du=−arsech⁡u+C=−arsech⁡(x−15)+C.
question.knowledge_point: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arsecant Integral

observed_steps.name: Question 7
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arsecant Integral
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{x}^{2}-8x & =-4({x}^{2}+2x) \\  & =-4({x}^{2}+2\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}) \\  & =-4[(x+1)^{2}-1] \\  & =4[1-(x+1)^{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{-4{x}^{2}-8x}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{4[1-(x+1)^{2}]}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x+1.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{-4{x}^{2}-8x}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x+1)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

−14arsech⁡(x+1)+C

12arcsch⁡(x+1)+C
Submit

EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: −4x2−8x=−4(x2+2x)=−4(x2+2⋅x+12−12)=−4[(x+1)2−1]=4[1−(x+1)2]

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫1(x+1)−4x2−8xdx=∫1(x+1)4[1−(x+1)2]dx=12∫1(x+1)1−(x+1)2dx.

Let u=x+1. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

∫1(x+1)−4x2−8xdx=12∫1(x+1)1−(x+1)2dx=12∫1u1−u2du=−12arsech⁡u+C=−12arsech⁡(x+1)+C.
question.knowledge_point: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arsecant Integral

observed_steps.name: Question 8
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arsecant Integral
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-4x-3 & =-({x}^{2}+4x+3) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}+3) \\  & =-((x+2)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x+2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x-3}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{1-(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x+2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x-3}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{1-(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x+2)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

∫1(x+2)−x2−4x−3dx=

a
−12arcsch⁡(x+2)+C
b
−12arsech⁡(x+2)+C
c
arcsch⁡(x+2)+C
d
−arsech⁡(x+2)+C
e
−2arsech⁡(x+2)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: −x2−4x−3=−(x2+4x+3)=−(x2+2⋅2x+22−22+3)=−((x+2)2−1)=1−(x+2)2

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫1(x+2)−x2−4x−3dx=∫1(x+2)1−(x+2)2dx.

Let u=x+2. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

∫1(x+2)−x2−4x−3dx=∫1(x+2)1−(x+2)2dx=∫1u1−u2du=−arsech⁡u+C=−arsech⁡(x+2)+C.
question.knowledge_point: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arsecant Integral

observed_steps.name: Question 9
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arsecant Integral
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}+10x-24 & =-({x}^{2}-10x+24) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 5x+{5}^{2}-{5}^{2}+24) \\  & =-((x-5)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x-5)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(3x-15)\sqrt{10x-{x}^{2}-24}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x-5)\sqrt{1-(x-5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-5.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(3x-15)\sqrt{10x-{x}^{2}-24}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x-5)\sqrt{1-(x-5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-5)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

∫1(3x−15)10x−x2−24dx=

a
−16arsech⁡(x−5)+C
b
16arsech⁡(x−5)+C
c
13arcsch⁡(x−5)+C
d
−16arcsch⁡(x−5)+C
e
−13arsech⁡(x−5)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: −x2+10x−24=−(x2−10x+24)=−(x2−2⋅5x+52−52+24)=−((x−5)2−1)=1−(x−5)2

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫1(3x−15)10x−x2−24dx=13∫1(x−5)1−(x−5)2dx.

Let u=x−5. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

∫1(3x−15)10x−x2−24dx=13∫1(x−5)1−(x−5)2dx=13∫1u1−u2du=−13arsech⁡u+C=−13arsech⁡(x−5)+C.

observed_steps.name: Question 10
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arsecant Integral
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-{x}^{2}-3 & =-({x}^{2}-4x+3) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}+3) \\  & =-((x-2)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{4x-{x}^{2}-3}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{1-(x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{4x-{x}^{2}-3}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{1-(x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-2)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=1

$$

$$

$$

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+4x+5 & =4({x}^{2}+x+\frac{5}{4}) \\  & =4({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{5}{4}) \\  & =4[{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+1]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{|2x+1|\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+4x+5}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{2}|\sqrt{4[1+{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}]}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x+\frac{1}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x+\frac{1}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

∫2|2x+1|4x2+4x+5dx=

a

b

−14arcsch⁡(x+12)+C

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

4x2+4x+5=4(x2+x+54)=4(x2+2⋅12x+(12)2−(12)2+54)=4[(x+12)2+1]

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫2|2x+1|4x2+4x+5dx=∫1|x+12|4[1+(x+12)2]dx=12∫1|x+12|1+(x+12)2dx.

Let u=x+12. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

12∫1|x+12|1+(x+12)2dx=12∫1|u|1+u2du=−12arcsch⁡u+C=−12arcsch⁡(x+12)+C.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcosecant Integral
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6x+13 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}+13 \\  & =(x+3)^{2}+4\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{6}{|x+3|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x+13}}\,\text{d}x & =-\int \frac{6}{|x+3|\sqrt{4+(x+3)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{6}{2|\frac{x+3}{2}|\sqrt{4+4{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+3}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+3}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+3}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =-\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =-3\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\frac{x+3}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
