EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

x2+6x+13=x2+2⋅3x+32−32+13=(x+3)2+4

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫−6|x+3|x2+6x+13dx=−∫6|x+3|4+(x+3)2dx=−∫62|x+32|4+4(x+32)2dx=−32∫1|x+32|1+(x+32)2dx.

Let u=x+32. Then, we have dudx=12⟹dx=2du.

Therefore,

−32∫1|x+32|1+(x+32)2dx=−32∫1|u|1+u2⋅2du=−3∫1|u|1+u2du=3arcsch⁡u+C=3arcsch⁡(x+32)+C.
question.knowledge_point: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcosecant Integral

observed_steps.name: Question 14
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcosecant Integral
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+5 & ={x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}+5 \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{2}{|4x-8|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-4x+5}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{2}{4|x-2|\sqrt{1+(x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|x-2|\sqrt{1+(x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|x-2|\sqrt{1+(x-2)^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x-2)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

∫2|4x−8|x2−4x+5dx=

a
−12arsech⁡(x−2)+C
b
12arsech⁡(x−2)+C
c
−2arcsch⁡(x−2)+C
d
−12arcsch⁡(x−2)+C
e
2arsech⁡(x−2)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

x2−4x+5=x2−2⋅2x+22−22+5=(x−2)2+1

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫2|4x−8|x2−4x+5dx=∫24|x−2|1+(x−2)2dx=12∫1|x−2|1+(x−2)2dx.

Let u=x−2. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

12∫1|x−2|1+(x−2)2dx=12∫1|u|1+u2du=−12arcsch⁡u+C=−12arcsch⁡(x−2)+C.
question.knowledge_point: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcosecant Integral

observed_steps.name: Question 15
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcosecant Integral
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x+5 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}+5 \\  & =(x+1)^{2}+4\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4}{|x+1|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+2x+5}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{4}{|x+1|\sqrt{4+(x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{2}{|\frac{x+1}{2}|\sqrt{4+4{(\frac{x+1}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+1}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+1}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+1}{2})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-2\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\frac{x+1}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

∫4|x+1|x2+2x+5dx=

a
−2arcsch⁡(x+12)+C
b
12arsech⁡(x+12)+C
c
−12arcsch⁡(x+12)+C
d
−4arcsch⁡(x+12)+C
e
2arsech⁡(x+12)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

x2+2x+5=x2+2⋅x+12−12+5=(x+1)2+4

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫4|x+1|x2+2x+5dx=∫4|x+1|4+(x+1)2dx=∫2|x+12|4+4(x+12)2dx=∫1|x+12|1+(x+12)2dx.

Let u=x+12. Then, we have dudx=12⟹dx=2du.

Therefore,

∫1|x+12|1+(x+12)2dx=∫1|u|1+u2⋅2du=2∫1|u|1+u2du=−2arcsch⁡u+C=−2arcsch⁡(x+12)+C.

observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcosecant Integral
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\eqalign{
3-2x-x^2 & = -(x^2 + 2x - 3)\[5pt]
& = -(x^2 + 2\cdot x +1^2 - 1^2 - 3)\[5pt]
& = -((x+1)^2 - 4) \[5pt]
&= 4 - (x+1)^2
}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \dfrac{1}{3-2x-x^2}\textrm{d}x =
\int \dfrac{1}{4-(x+1)^2}\textrm{d}x = 
\dfrac{1}{4} {\int}\dfrac{1}{ 1 - \left( \frac{1}{2}(x+1)\right)^2 }\textrm{d}x.
$$

Let $u = \dfrac{1}{2}(x+1).$ Then, we have

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}u}{\textrm{d}x}=\dfrac{1}{2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\textrm{d}x = 2\,\textrm{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{2}(x+1))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{2}(x+1))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+1}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $\left|\dfrac {x+1} {2} \right| >   1.$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-4x-{x}^{2} & =-({x}^{2}+4x-1) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}-1) \\  & =-((x+2)^{2}-5) \\  & =5-(x+2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-4x-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{5-(x+2)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2))+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{5}})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{5}}|>1.$

Question 16
?

∫11−4x−x2dx=

a
15arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
b
−15arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
c
15arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
d
−55arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
e
55arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the denominator: 1−4x−x2=−(x2+4x−1)=−(x2+2⋅2x+22−22−1)=−((x+2)2−5)=5−(x+2)2

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get ∫11−4x−x2dx=∫15−(x+2)2dx=15∫11−(15(x+2))2dx.

Let u=15(x+2). Then, we have dudx=15⟹dx=5du.

Therefore, 15∫11−(15(x+2))2dx=15∫11−u2⋅5du=55∫11−u2du=55⋅arcoth⁡u+C=55⋅arcoth⁡(15(x+2))+C=55arcoth⁡(x+25)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x+25|>1.
question.knowledge_point: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral

observed_steps.name: Question 17
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{1}{9-(x+4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{9-9(\frac{1}{9}(x+4)^{2})}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{3}(x+4))}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{3}(x+4).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{3}(x+4))}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{9}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+4}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x+4}{3}|>1.$

question.name: Question 17
question.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{9-(x+4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=$
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{1}{9-(x+4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{9-9(\frac{1}{9}(x+4)^{2})}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{3}(x+4))}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{3}(x+4).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{3}(x+4))}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{9}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+4}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x+4}{3}|>1.$

EXPLANATION

First, we note that ∫19−(x+4)2dx=∫19−9(19(x+4)2)dx=19∫11−(13(x+4))2dx.

Let u=13(x+4). Then, we have

dudx=13⟹dx=3du.

question.knowledge_point: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral

observed_steps.name: Question 18
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x-{x}^{2}-5 & =-({x}^{2}-6x+5) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}+5) \\  & =-((x-3)^{2}-4) \\  & =4-(x-3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{6x-{x}^{2}-5}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{4-(x-3)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{2}(x-3))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{2}(x-3).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{2}(x-3))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{2}(x-3))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x-3}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x-3}{2}|>1.$

Question 18
?

∫16x−x2−5dx=

a
22arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
b
22arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
c
12arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
d
−22arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
e
−12arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the denominator: 6x−x2−5=−(x2−6x+5)=−(x2−2⋅3x+32−32+5)=−((x−3)2−4)=4−(x−3)2

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get ∫16x−x2−5dx=∫14−(x−3)2dx=14∫11−(12(x−3))2dx.

Let u=12(x−3). Then, we have dudx=12⟹dx=2du.

Therefore, 14∫11−(12(x−3))2dx=14∫11−u2⋅2du=12∫11−u2du=12⋅arcoth⁡u+C=12⋅arcoth⁡(12(x−3))+C=12arcoth⁡(x−32)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x−32|>1.
question.knowledge_point: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral

observed_steps.name: Question 19
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}12x-{x}^{2}-33 & =-({x}^{2}-12x+33) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 6x+{6}^{2}-{6}^{2}+33) \\  & =-((x-6)^{2}-3) \\  & =3-(x-6)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{12x-{x}^{2}-33}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{3-(x-6)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6))+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x-6}{\sqrt{3}})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x-6}{\sqrt{3}}|>1.$

EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the denominator: 12x−x2−33=−(x2−12x+33)=−(x2−2⋅6x+62−62+33)=−((x−6)2−3)=3−(x−6)2

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get ∫112x−x2−33dx=∫13−(x−6)2dx=13∫11−(13(x−6))2dx.

Let u=13(x−6). Then, we have dudx=13⟹dx=3du.

Therefore, 13∫11−(13(x−6))2dx=13∫11−u2⋅3du=33∫11−u2du=33⋅arcoth⁡u+C=33⋅arcoth⁡(13(x−6))+C=33arcoth⁡(x−63)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x−63|>1.
question.knowledge_point: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral

observed_steps.name: Question 20
observed_steps.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral
observed_steps.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}12+4x-{x}^{2} & =-({x}^{2}-4x-12) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}-12) \\  & =-((x-2)^{2}-16) \\  & =16-(x-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{12+4x-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{16-(x-2)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{4}(x-2))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{4}(x-2).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{4}(x-2))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 4\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{4}(x-2))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x-2}{4})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x-2}{4}|>1.$

Question 20
?

∫112+4x−x2dx=

a
18arcoth⁡(x−24)+C
b
14arcoth⁡(x−22)+C
c
14arcoth⁡(x−24)+C
d
116arcoth⁡(x−24)+C
e
−116arcoth⁡(x−22)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the denominator: 12+4x−x2=−(x2−4x−12)=−(x2−2⋅2x+22−22−12)=−((x−2)2−16)=16−(x−2)2

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get ∫112+4x−x2dx=∫116−(x−2)2dx=116∫11−(14(x−2))2dx.

Let u=14(x−2). Then, we have dudx=14⟹dx=4du.

Therefore, 116∫11−(14(x−2))2dx=116∫11−u2⋅4du=14∫11−u2du=14⋅arcoth⁡u+C=14⋅arcoth⁡(14(x−2))+C=14arcoth⁡(x−24)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x−24|>1.

Thus d is valid on -1<x<0. On -2<x<-1, a real antiderivative requires arsech(|x+1|); the source omits this domain qualification.

Since -4x²-8x=4[1-(x+1)²], substitution u=x+1 gives (1/2)∫du/(u√(1-u²))=-(1/2)arsech(u)+C for 0<u<1. Thus b is valid on -1<x<0. On -2<x<-1, use arsech(|x+1|); the source omits this domain qualification.

My earlier answer d was submitted and graded Correct, and matches the worked solution. Since -x²-4x-3=1-(x+2)², setting u=x+2 gives ∫du/(u√(1-u²))=-arsech(u)+C for 0<u<1. Thus d is valid on -2<x<-1. Thus d is valid on 2<x<3. On 1<x<2, a real antiderivative requires arsech(|x-2|); the source omits this domain qualification.

The worked solution confirms my earlier answer c. The Incorrect grade applies to submitted option a, whose coefficient is one third of the required value. With u=x+1/3, the denominator is 9|u|√(1+u²), so the integral becomes (1/3)∫du/(|u|√(1+u²))=-(1/3)arcsch(u)+C, valid for x≠-1/3.

My earlier answer a was submitted and graded Correct, and matches the worked solution. With u=x+1/2, |2x+1|=2|u| and √(4x²+4x+5)=2√(1+u²). The integral becomes (1/2)∫du/(|u|√(1+u²))=-(1/2)arcsch(u)+C, valid for x≠-1/2.

The worked solution confirms my earlier answer e. The Incorrect grade applies to submitted option a, which uses arsech instead of arcsch. Completing the square and setting u=(x+3)/2 reduces the integral to -3∫du/(|u|√(1+u²))=3 arcsch(u)+C, valid for x≠-3.

My earlier answer d was submitted and graded Correct, and matches the worked solution. Since x²-4x+5=(x-2)²+1 and |4x-8|=4|x-2|, setting u=x-2 reduces the integral to (1/2)∫du/(|u|√(1+u²))=-(1/2)arcsch(u)+C, valid for x≠2.

My earlier answer a was submitted and graded Correct, and matches the worked solution. Completing the square gives x²+2x+5=(x+1)²+4. Substituting u=(x+1)/2 reduces the integral to 2∫du/(|u|√(1+u²))=-2 arcsch(u)+C, valid for x≠-1.

My earlier answer e was submitted and graded Correct, and matches the worked solution. Completing the square gives 5-(x+2)². Substituting u=(x+2)/√5 yields (√5/5)∫du/(1-u²)=(√5/5)arcoth(u)+C. The source correctly restricts this real expression to |x+2|>√5.

The worked solution confirms my earlier answer b. The Incorrect grade applies to submitted option a, whose coefficient is nine times too large. Substituting u=(x+4)/3 gives (1/3)∫du/(1-u²)=(1/3)arcoth(u)+C. The source correctly restricts this real expression to |x+4|>3.

My earlier answer c was submitted and graded Correct, and matches the worked solution. Completing the square gives 4-(x-3)². Substituting u=(x-3)/2 yields (1/2)∫du/(1-u²)=(1/2)arcoth(u)+C. The source correctly restricts this real expression to |x-3|>2, meaning x<1 or x>5.

The worked solution confirms my earlier answer b. The Incorrect grade applies to submitted option a, which omits a factor of √3. Completing the square gives 3-(x-6)²; substituting u=(x-6)/√3 yields (√3/3)∫du/(1-u²)=(√3/3)arcoth(u)+C. The source correctly restricts this real expression to |x-6|>√3.

My earlier answer c was submitted and graded Correct, and matches the worked solution. Completing the square gives 16-(x-2)². Substituting u=(x-2)/4 yields (1/4)∫du/(1-u²)=(1/4)arcoth(u)+C. The source correctly restricts this real expression to |x-2|>4, meaning x<-2 or x>6.

The worked example has no answer fields. Its stated antiderivative, (1/4)arcoth(x-1)+C, is correct under its explicit restriction |x-1|>1. Indeed, substituting u=x-1 reduces the integral to (1/4)∫du/(1-u²). My earlier mathematical judgment stands; the invented answer field was inappropriate.

With u=x-1, the integral becomes ∫du/(u√(1-u²)). Math Academy's stated -arsech(x-1)+C is correct on 1<x<2. Its omitted domain qualification matters: on 0<x<1 this expression is not real. A real antiderivative covering both intervals is -arsech(|x-1|)+C, with independent constants. There are no current answer fields.

Since |3x+9|=3|x+3| and x²+6x+10=(x+3)²+1, substituting u=x+3 gives 2∫du/(|u|√(1+u²))=-2 arcsch(u)+C. Math Academy's stated -2 arcsch(x+3)+C is correct for x≠-3, with independent constants on the two intervals. There are no current answer fields.

Completing the square gives 3-2x-x²=4-(x+1)². Setting u=(x+1)/2 reduces the integral to (1/2)∫du/(1-u²), giving Math Academy's stated (1/2)arcoth((x+1)/2)+C. Its explicit restriction |(x+1)/2|>1 correctly makes this a real antiderivative on x<-3 or x>1. There are no current answer fields.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|6x-2|\sqrt{9+(3x-1)^{2}}}.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|6x-2|\sqrt{9+(3x-1)^{2}}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{6|x-\frac{1}{3}|\sqrt{9+9{(x-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{|x-\frac{1}{3}|\sqrt{1+{(x-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-\frac{1}{3}.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{|x-\frac{1}{3}|\sqrt{1+{(x-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x-\frac{1}{3})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\frac{3x-1}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Calculate ∫dx|6x−2|9+(3x−1)2.

a
19arsech⁡(3x−13)+C
b
−19arcsch⁡(3x−1)+C
c
−118arcsch⁡(3x−13)+C
d
−118arsech⁡(3x−13)+C
e
118arcsch⁡(3x−1)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that ∫dx|6x−2|9+(3x−1)2=∫dx6|x−13|9+9(x−13)2=118∫1|x−13|1+(x−13)2dx.

Let u=x−13. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore, 118∫1|x−13|1+(x−13)2dx=118∫1|u|1+u2du=−118arcsch⁡u+C=−118arcsch⁡(x−13)+C=−118arcsch⁡(3x−13)+C.

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{|6x-2|\sqrt{9+(3x-1)^{2}}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{6|x-\frac{1}{3}|\sqrt{9+9{(x-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{|x-\frac{1}{3}|\sqrt{1+{(x-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-\frac{1}{3}.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{|x-\frac{1}{3}|\sqrt{1+{(x-\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x-\frac{1}{3})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\frac{3x-1}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(6x-4)\sqrt{9-(3x-2)^{2}}}.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(6x-4)\sqrt{9-(3x-2)^{2}}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{6(x-\frac{2}{3})\sqrt{9-9{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})\sqrt{1-{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-\frac{2}{3}.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})\sqrt{1-{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-\frac{2}{3})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(\frac{3x-2}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Calculate ∫dx(6x−4)9−(3x−2)2.

a
19arsech⁡(3x−2)+C
b
−118arcsch⁡(3x−2)+C
c
−118arsech⁡(3x−23)+C
d
118arcsch⁡(3x−23)+C
e
−19arsech⁡(3x−23)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that ∫dx(6x−4)9−(3x−2)2=∫dx6(x−23)9−9(x−23)2=118∫1(x−23)1−(x−23)2dx.

Let u=x−23. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore, 118∫1(x−23)1−(x−23)2dx=118∫1u1−u2du=−118arsech⁡u+C=−118arsech⁡(x−23)+C=−118arsech⁡(3x−23)+C.

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing an Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Integral Containing a Completed Square
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(6x-4)\sqrt{9-(3x-2)^{2}}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{6(x-\frac{2}{3})\sqrt{9-9{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})\sqrt{1-{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-\frac{2}{3}.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})\sqrt{1-{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-\frac{2}{3})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(\frac{3x-2}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we note that ∫dx(6x−4)9−(3x−2)2=∫dx6(x−23)9−9(x−23)2=118∫1(x−23)1−(x−23)2dx.

Let u=x−23. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore, 118∫1(x−23)1−(x−23)2dx=118∫1u1−u2du=−118arsech⁡u+C=−118arsech⁡(x−23)+C=−118arsech⁡(3x−23)+C.
question.knowledge_point: Computing an Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Integral Containing a Completed Square

solution.reasoning: Set u=(3x-2)/3; then dx=du and the integral becomes (1/18)∫du/(u√(1-u²)). For 0<u<1 this equals -(1/18)arsech(u)+C, giving option c. On the full real integrand domain, the antiderivative is -(1/18)arsech(|u|)+C, with constants chosen separately on each interval. Thus option c requires 2/3<x<5/3; no listed choice covers the negative-u interval as a real expression. No Math Academy answer evidence for this question was captured.

feedback.name: Question 2
feedback.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(6x-4)\sqrt{9-(3x-2)^{2}}}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(6x-4)\sqrt{9-(3x-2)^{2}}}=\int \frac{\text{d}x}{6(x-\frac{2}{3})\sqrt{9-9{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})\sqrt{1-{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-\frac{2}{3}.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{(x-\frac{2}{3})\sqrt{1-{(x-\frac{2}{3})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{18}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-\frac{2}{3})+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{18}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(\frac{3x-2}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{4-(x+3)^{2}}\text{d}x.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{1}{4-(x+3)^{2}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{4-4{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+3}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+3}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x+3}{2}|>1.$

Question 3
?

Calculate ∫14−(x+3)2dx.

a
12arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
b
12arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
c
14arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
d
2arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
e
14arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that ∫14−(x+3)2dx=∫14−4(x+32)2dx=14∫11−(x+32)2dx.

Let u=x+32. Then, we have dudx=12⟹dx=2du.

Therefore, 14∫11−(x+32)2dx=14∫11−u2⋅2du=12∫11−u2du=12⋅arcoth⁡u+C=12arcoth⁡(x+32)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x+32|>1.

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing an Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Integral Containing a Completed Square
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{1}{4-(x+3)^{2}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{4-4{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+3}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+3}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x+3}{2}|>1.$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Calculate ∫14−(x+3)2dx.

a
12arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
b
12arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
c
14arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
d
2arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
e
14arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that ∫14−(x+3)2dx=∫14−4(x+32)2dx=14∫11−(x+32)2dx.

Let u=x+32. Then, we have dudx=12⟹dx=2du.

Therefore, 14∫11−(x+32)2dx=14∫11−u2⋅2du=12∫11−u2du=12⋅arcoth⁡u+C=12arcoth⁡(x+32)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x+32|>1.
question.knowledge_point: Computing an Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Integral Containing a Completed Square

solution.reasoning: Let u=(x+3)/2, so dx=2 du. The integral becomes (1/2)∫du/(1-u²)=(1/2)arcoth(u)+C for |u|>1, yielding option b. This real arcoth form applies when x<-5 or x>-1. On -5<x<-1, use (1/2)artanh(u)+C; a logarithmic form valid on all intervals is (1/4)ln|(x+5)/(x+1)|+C. The supplied example supports the integration method but does not establish Math Academy's answer for this question.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{4-(x+3)^{2}}\text{d}x.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{1}{4-(x+3)^{2}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{4-4{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+3}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+3}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x+3}{2}|>1.$

Question 3

Calculate ∫14−(x+3)2dx.

a
12arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
b
12arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
c
14arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
d
2arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
e
14arcoth⁡(x+32)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that ∫14−(x+3)2dx=∫14−4(x+32)2dx=14∫11−(x+32)2dx.

Let u=x+32. Then, we have dudx=12⟹dx=2du.

Therefore, 14∫11−(x+32)2dx=14∫11−u2⋅2du=12∫11−u2du=12⋅arcoth⁡u+C=12arcoth⁡(x+32)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x+32|>1.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x+1)\sqrt{9-(3x+3)^{2}}}.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x+1)\sqrt{9-(3x+3)^{2}}} & =\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x+1)\sqrt{9-9{(x+1)}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x+1.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x+1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculate ∫dx(x+1)9−(3x+3)2.

a
16arcsch⁡(3x+1)+C
b
3arcsch⁡(x+1)+C
c
−13arsech⁡(3x+1)+C
d
−13arsech⁡(x+1)+C
e
−16arsech⁡(x+1)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

∫dx(x+1)9−(3x+3)2=∫dx(x+1)9−9(x+1)2=13∫1(x+1)1−(x+1)2dx.

Let u=x+1. Then, we have

dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore, 13∫1(x+1)1−(x+1)2dx=13∫1u1−u2⋅du=−13arsech⁡u+C=−13arsech⁡(x+1)+C.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing an Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Integral Containing a Completed Square
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x+1)\sqrt{9-(3x+3)^{2}}} & =\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x+1)\sqrt{9-9{(x+1)}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x+1.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x+1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Calculate ∫dx(x+1)9−(3x+3)2.

a
16arcsch⁡(3x+1)+C
b
3arcsch⁡(x+1)+C
c
−13arsech⁡(3x+1)+C
d
−13arsech⁡(x+1)+C
e
−16arsech⁡(x+1)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

∫dx(x+1)9−(3x+3)2=∫dx(x+1)9−9(x+1)2=13∫1(x+1)1−(x+1)2dx.

Let u=x+1. Then, we have

dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore, 13∫1(x+1)1−(x+1)2dx=13∫1u1−u2⋅du=−13arsech⁡u+C=−13arsech⁡(x+1)+C.
question.knowledge_point: Computing an Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Integral Containing a Completed Square

solution.reasoning: Let u=x+1. Since √(9-(3x+3)²)=3√(1-u²), the integral is (1/3)∫du/(u√(1-u²))=-(1/3)arsech(u)+C for 0<u<1. Thus select d, valid for -1<x<0. On both real domain intervals, a general expression is -(1/3)arsech(|x+1|)+C, with independent constants on (-2,-1) and (-1,0). feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x+1)\sqrt{9-(3x+3)^{2}}}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x+1)\sqrt{9-(3x+3)^{2}}} & =\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x+1)\sqrt{9-9{(x+1)}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x+1.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x+1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

∫dx(x+1)9−(3x+3)2=∫dx(x+1)9−9(x+1)2=13∫1(x+1)1−(x+1)2dx.

feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Computing an Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Integral Containing a Completed Square

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x-1)\sqrt{4-(2x-2)^{2}}}.$
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x-1)\sqrt{4-(2x-2)^{2}}} & =\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x-1)\sqrt{4-4{(x-1)}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{1-(x-1)^{2}}}\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x-1.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{1-(x-1)^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Calculate ∫dx(x−1)4−(2x−2)2.

a
14arsech⁡(x−1)+C
b
−12arsech⁡(x−1)+C
c
14arcsch⁡(2x−2)+C
d
−12arsech⁡(2x−1)+C
e
2arcsch⁡(x−1)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

∫dx(x−1)4−(2x−2)2=∫dx(x−1)4−4(x−1)2=12∫1(x−1)1−(x−1)2dx.

Let u=x−1. Then, we have

dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore, 12∫1(x−1)1−(x−1)2dx=12∫1u1−u2⋅du=−12arsech⁡u+C=−12arsech⁡(x−1)+C.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Computing an Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Integral Containing a Completed Square
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x-1)\sqrt{4-(2x-2)^{2}}} & =\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x-1)\sqrt{4-4{(x-1)}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{1-(x-1)^{2}}}\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x-1.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{1-(x-1)^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Calculate ∫dx(x−1)4−(2x−2)2.

a
14arsech⁡(x−1)+C
b
−12arsech⁡(x−1)+C
c
14arcsch⁡(2x−2)+C
d
−12arsech⁡(2x−1)+C
e
2arcsch⁡(x−1)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we note that

∫dx(x−1)4−(2x−2)2=∫dx(x−1)4−4(x−1)2=12∫1(x−1)1−(x−1)2dx.

Let u=x−1. Then, we have

dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore, 12∫1(x−1)1−(x−1)2dx=12∫1u1−u2⋅du=−12arsech⁡u+C=−12arsech⁡(x−1)+C.
question.knowledge_point: Computing an Inverse Reciprocal Hyperbolic Integral Containing a Completed Square

solution.reasoning: Let u=x-1. The integral becomes (1/2)∫du/(u√(1-u²))=-(1/2)arsech(u)+C for 0<u<1, so option b is correct on 1<x<2. A real antiderivative covering both domain intervals is -(1/2)arsech(|x-1|)+C, with independent constants on (0,1) and (1,2). No Math Academy answer evidence for this question was captured.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x-1)\sqrt{4-(2x-2)^{2}}}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x-1)\sqrt{4-(2x-2)^{2}}} & =\int \frac{\text{d}x}{(x-1)\sqrt{4-4{(x-1)}^{2}}}=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{1-(x-1)^{2}}}\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x-1.$ Then, we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x-1)\sqrt{1-(x-1)^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-1)+C.\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: $\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{(x-1)\sqrt{4+2x-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x=$
question.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}+2x+4 & =-({x}^{2}-2x-4) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}-4) \\  & =-((x-1)^{2}-5) \\  & =5-(x-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{(x-1)\sqrt{4+2x-{x}^{2}}} & =\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{(x-1)\sqrt{5-{(x-1)}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})\sqrt{5-5{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{(x-1)\sqrt{4+2x-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

∫5(x−1)4+2x−x2dx=

a
−arsech⁡(x−15)+C
b
15arcsch⁡(x−15)+C
c
−15arsech⁡(x−15)+C
d
−5arsech⁡(x−15)+C
e
arcsch⁡(x−15)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: −x2+2x+4=−(x2−2x−4)=−(x2−2⋅x+12−12−4)=−((x−1)2−5)=5−(x−1)2

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫5(x−1)4+2x−x2=∫5(x−1)5−(x−1)2dx=∫1(x−15)5−5(x−15)2dx=15∫1(x−15)1−(x−15)2dx.

Let u=x−15. Then, we have dudx=15⟹dx=5du.

Therefore,

∫5(x−1)4+2x−x2dx=15∫1(x−15)1−(x−15)2dx=15∫1u1−u2⋅5du=∫1u1−u2du=−arsech⁡u+C=−arsech⁡(x−15)+C.

last_observation.name: Question 6
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arsecant Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}+2x+4 & =-({x}^{2}-2x-4) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}-4) \\  & =-((x-1)^{2}-5) \\  & =5-(x-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{(x-1)\sqrt{4+2x-{x}^{2}}} & =\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{(x-1)\sqrt{5-{(x-1)}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})\sqrt{5-5{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{(x-1)\sqrt{4+2x-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 6
?

∫5(x−1)4+2x−x2dx=

a
−arsech⁡(x−15)+C
b
15arcsch⁡(x−15)+C
c
−15arsech⁡(x−15)+C
d
−5arsech⁡(x−15)+C
e
arcsch⁡(x−15)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: −x2+2x+4=−(x2−2x−4)=−(x2−2⋅x+12−12−4)=−((x−1)2−5)=5−(x−1)2

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫5(x−1)4+2x−x2=∫5(x−1)5−(x−1)2dx=∫1(x−15)5−5(x−15)2dx=15∫1(x−15)1−(x−15)2dx.

Let u=x−15. Then, we have dudx=15⟹dx=5du.

Therefore,

∫5(x−1)4+2x−x2dx=15∫1(x−15)1−(x−15)2dx=15∫1u1−u2⋅5du=∫1u1−u2du=−arsech⁡u+C=−arsech⁡(x−15)+C.
question.knowledge_point: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arsecant Integral

solution.reasoning: Complete the square: 4+2x-x²=5-(x-1)². With u=(x-1)/√5 and dx=√5 du, the integral becomes ∫du/(u√(1-u²))=-arsech(u)+C for 0<u<1. Thus option a is correct on 1<x<1+√5. Across both real domain intervals, use -arsech(|x-1|/√5)+C with separate constants. The supplied example establishes the method but does not capture Math Academy's answer for this question.

feedback.name: Question 6
feedback.problem: $\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{(x-1)\sqrt{4+2x-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x=$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}+2x+4 & =-({x}^{2}-2x-4) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}-4) \\  & =-((x-1)^{2}-5) \\  & =5-(x-1)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{(x-1)\sqrt{4+2x-{x}^{2}}} & =\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{(x-1)\sqrt{5-{(x-1)}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})\sqrt{5-5{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{\sqrt{5}}{(x-1)\sqrt{4+2x-{x}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{1}{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})\sqrt{1-{(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\cdot \sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(\frac{x-1}{\sqrt{5}})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 7
question.problem: $\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{-4{x}^{2}-8x}}\text{d}x=$
question.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{x}^{2}-8x & =-4({x}^{2}+2x) \\  & =-4({x}^{2}+2\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}) \\  & =-4[(x+1)^{2}-1] \\  & =4[1-(x+1)^{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{-4{x}^{2}-8x}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{4[1-(x+1)^{2}]}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x+1.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{-4{x}^{2}-8x}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x+1)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

∫1(x+1)−4x2−8xdx=

a
−4arsech⁡(x+1)+C
b
−12arsech⁡(x+1)+C
c
−14arsech⁡(x+1)+C

−12arcsch⁡(x+1)+C

12arcsch⁡(x+1)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: −4x2−8x=−4(x2+2x)=−4(x2+2⋅x+12−12)=−4[(x+1)2−1]=4[1−(x+1)2]

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫1(x+1)−4x2−8xdx=∫1(x+1)4[1−(x+1)2]dx=12∫1(x+1)1−(x+1)2dx.

Let u=x+1. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

∫1(x+1)−4x2−8xdx=12∫1(x+1)1−(x+1)2dx=12∫1u1−u2du=−12arsech⁡u+C=−12arsech⁡(x+1)+C.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arsecant Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{x}^{2}-8x & =-4({x}^{2}+2x) \\  & =-4({x}^{2}+2\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}) \\  & =-4[(x+1)^{2}-1] \\  & =4[1-(x+1)^{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{-4{x}^{2}-8x}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{4[1-(x+1)^{2}]}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x+1.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{-4{x}^{2}-8x}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x+1)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

∫1(x+1)−4x2−8xdx=

a
−4arsech⁡(x+1)+C
b
−12arsech⁡(x+1)+C
c
−14arsech⁡(x+1)+C

−12arcsch⁡(x+1)+C

12arcsch⁡(x+1)+C
Submit

EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: −4x2−8x=−4(x2+2x)=−4(x2+2⋅x+12−12)=−4[(x+1)2−1]=4[1−(x+1)2]

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫1(x+1)−4x2−8xdx=∫1(x+1)4[1−(x+1)2]dx=12∫1(x+1)1−(x+1)2dx.

Let u=x+1. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

∫1(x+1)−4x2−8xdx=12∫1(x+1)1−(x+1)2dx=12∫1u1−u2du=−12arsech⁡u+C=−12arsech⁡(x+1)+C.
question.knowledge_point: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arsecant Integral

solution.reasoning: Complete the square: -4x²-8x=4(1-(x+1)²). Setting u=x+1 gives (1/2)∫du/(u√(1-u²))=-(1/2)arsech(u)+C for 0<u<1. Thus option b is correct on -1<x<0. A real antiderivative on both domain intervals is -(1/2)arsech(|x+1|)+C, with independent constants on (-2,-1) and (-1,0). No Math Academy answer evidence for this question was captured.

feedback.name: Question 7
feedback.problem: $\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{-4{x}^{2}-8x}}\text{d}x=$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-4{x}^{2}-8x & =-4({x}^{2}+2x) \\  & =-4({x}^{2}+2\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}) \\  & =-4[(x+1)^{2}-1] \\  & =4[1-(x+1)^{2}]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{-4{x}^{2}-8x}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{4[1-(x+1)^{2}]}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x+1.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{-4{x}^{2}-8x}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{(x+1)\sqrt{1-(x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x+1)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: −4x2−8x=−4(x2+2x)=−4(x2+2⋅x+12−12)=−4[(x+1)2−1]=4[1−(x+1)2]

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫1(x+1)−4x2−8xdx=∫1(x+1)4[1−(x+1)2]dx=12∫1(x+1)1−(x+1)2dx.

Let u=x+1. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

∫1(x+1)−4x2−8xdx=12∫1(x+1)1−(x+1)2dx=12∫1u1−u2du=−12arsech⁡u+C=−12arsech⁡(x+1)+C.

question.name: Question 8
question.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-4x-3 & =-({x}^{2}+4x+3) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}+3) \\  & =-((x+2)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x+2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x-3}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{1-(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x+2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x-3}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{1-(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x+2)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-4x-3 & =-({x}^{2}+4x+3) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}+3) \\  & =-((x+2)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x+2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x-3}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{1-(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x+2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x-3}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{1-(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x+2)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

∫1(x+2)−x2−4x−3dx=

a
−12arcsch⁡(x+2)+C
b
−12arsech⁡(x+2)+C
c
arcsch⁡(x+2)+C
d
−arsech⁡(x+2)+C
e
−2arsech⁡(x+2)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: −x2−4x−3=−(x2+4x+3)=−(x2+2⋅2x+22−22+3)=−((x+2)2−1)=1−(x+2)2

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫1(x+2)−x2−4x−3dx=∫1(x+2)1−(x+2)2dx.

Let u=x+2. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

∫1(x+2)−x2−4x−3dx=∫1(x+2)1−(x+2)2dx=∫1u1−u2du=−arsech⁡u+C=−arsech⁡(x+2)+C.
question.knowledge_point: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arsecant Integral

solution.reasoning: Complete the square: -x²-4x-3=1-(x+2)². With u=x+2, the integral becomes ∫du/(u√(1-u²))=-arsech(u)+C for 0<u<1, yielding option d on -2<x<-1. A real antiderivative on both domain intervals is -arsech(|x+2|)+C, with independent constants on (-3,-2) and (-2,-1). No Math Academy answer evidence for this question was captured.

feedback.name: Question 8
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}-4x-3 & =-({x}^{2}+4x+3) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}+3) \\  & =-((x+2)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x+2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x-3}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{1-(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x+2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{-{x}^{2}-4x-3}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x+2)\sqrt{1-(x+2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x+2)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 9
question.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}+10x-24 & =-({x}^{2}-10x+24) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 5x+{5}^{2}-{5}^{2}+24) \\  & =-((x-5)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x-5)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(3x-15)\sqrt{10x-{x}^{2}-24}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x-5)\sqrt{1-(x-5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-5.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(3x-15)\sqrt{10x-{x}^{2}-24}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x-5)\sqrt{1-(x-5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-5)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

∫1(3x−15)10x−x2−24dx=

a
−16arsech⁡(x−5)+C
b
16arsech⁡(x−5)+C
c
13arcsch⁡(x−5)+C
d
−16arcsch⁡(x−5)+C
e
−13arsech⁡(x−5)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: −x2+10x−24=−(x2−10x+24)=−(x2−2⋅5x+52−52+24)=−((x−5)2−1)=1−(x−5)2

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫1(3x−15)10x−x2−24dx=13∫1(x−5)1−(x−5)2dx.

Let u=x−5. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

∫1(3x−15)10x−x2−24dx=13∫1(x−5)1−(x−5)2dx=13∫1u1−u2du=−13arsech⁡u+C=−13arsech⁡(x−5)+C.

last_observation.name: Question 9
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arsecant Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}+10x-24 & =-({x}^{2}-10x+24) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 5x+{5}^{2}-{5}^{2}+24) \\  & =-((x-5)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x-5)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(3x-15)\sqrt{10x-{x}^{2}-24}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x-5)\sqrt{1-(x-5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-5.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(3x-15)\sqrt{10x-{x}^{2}-24}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x-5)\sqrt{1-(x-5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-5)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

∫1(3x−15)10x−x2−24dx=

a
−16arsech⁡(x−5)+C
b
16arsech⁡(x−5)+C
c
13arcsch⁡(x−5)+C
d
−16arcsch⁡(x−5)+C
e
−13arsech⁡(x−5)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: −x2+10x−24=−(x2−10x+24)=−(x2−2⋅5x+52−52+24)=−((x−5)2−1)=1−(x−5)2

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫1(3x−15)10x−x2−24dx=13∫1(x−5)1−(x−5)2dx.

Let u=x−5. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

∫1(3x−15)10x−x2−24dx=13∫1(x−5)1−(x−5)2dx=13∫1u1−u2du=−13arsech⁡u+C=−13arsech⁡(x−5)+C.
question.knowledge_point: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arsecant Integral

solution.reasoning: Complete the square: 10x-x²-24=1-(x-5)², and 3x-15=3(x-5). Setting u=x-5 gives (1/3)∫du/(u√(1-u²))=-(1/3)arsech(u)+C for 0<u<1. Thus select e, valid on 5<x<6. On both real domain intervals, use -(1/3)arsech(|x-5|)+C, with independent constants on (4,5) and (5,6). No Math Academy answer evidence for this question was captured.

feedback.name: Question 9
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}-{x}^{2}+10x-24 & =-({x}^{2}-10x+24) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 5x+{5}^{2}-{5}^{2}+24) \\  & =-((x-5)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x-5)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(3x-15)\sqrt{10x-{x}^{2}-24}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x-5)\sqrt{1-(x-5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-5.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(3x-15)\sqrt{10x-{x}^{2}-24}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{(x-5)\sqrt{1-(x-5)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-5)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.problem: $\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{4x-{x}^{2}-3}}\text{d}x=$
question.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-{x}^{2}-3 & =-({x}^{2}-4x+3) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}+3) \\  & =-((x-2)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{4x-{x}^{2}-3}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{1-(x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{4x-{x}^{2}-3}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{1-(x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-2)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arsecant Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}4x-{x}^{2}-3 & =-({x}^{2}-4x+3) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}+3) \\  & =-((x-2)^{2}-1) \\  & =1-(x-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{4x-{x}^{2}-3}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{1-(x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{4x-{x}^{2}-3}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{(x-2)\sqrt{1-(x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{u\sqrt{1-{u}^{2}}}\text{d}u \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡u+C \\  & =-\operatorname{arsech}⁡(x-2)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

∫1(x−2)4x−x2−3dx=

a
arcsch⁡(x−2)+C
b
−4arsech⁡(x−2)+C
c
−14arsech⁡(x−2)+C
d
−arsech⁡(x−2)+C
e
−12arcsch⁡(x−2)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: 4x−x2−3=−(x2−4x+3)=−(x2−2⋅2x+22−22+3)=−((x−2)2−1)=1−(x−2)2

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫1(x−2)4x−x2−3dx=∫1(x−2)1−(x−2)2dx.

Let u=x−2. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

∫1(x−2)4x−x2−3dx=∫1(x−2)1−(x−2)2dx=∫1u1−u2du=−arsech⁡u+C=−arsech⁡(x−2)+C.

solution.reasoning: Complete the square: 4x-x²-3=1-(x-2)². With u=x-2, the integral becomes ∫du/(u√(1-u²))=-arsech(u)+C for 0<u<1. Thus option d is correct on 2<x<3. A real antiderivative covering both domain intervals is -arsech(|x-2|)+C, with independent constants on (1,2) and (2,3). No Math Academy answer evidence for this question was captured.

arcsch⁡(x−2)+C

−4arsech⁡(x−2)+C

−14arsech⁡(x−2)+C

EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator: 4x−x2−3=−(x2−4x+3)=−(x2−2⋅2x+22−22+3)=−((x−2)2−1)=1−(x−2)2

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫1(x−2)4x−x2−3dx=∫1(x−2)1−(x−2)2dx.

Let u=x−2. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

∫1(x−2)4x−x2−3dx=∫1(x−2)1−(x−2)2dx=∫1u1−u2du=−arsech⁡u+C=−arsech⁡(x−2)+C.

question.name: Question 11
question.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}+6x+10 & =9({x}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{10}{9}) \\  & =9({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{3}x+{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}+\frac{10}{9}) \\  & =9[{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2}+1]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{|3x+1|\sqrt{9{x}^{2}+6x+10}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{3}|\sqrt{9[1+{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2}]}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{3}|\sqrt{1+{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x+\frac{1}{3}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{3}|\sqrt{1+{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x+\frac{1}{3})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

∫3|3x+1|9x2+6x+10dx=

a
−19arcsch⁡(x+13)+C
b
−3arcsch⁡(x+13)+C
c
−13arcsch⁡(x+13)+C
d
3arsech⁡(x+13)+C
e
13arsech⁡(x+13)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

9x2+6x+10=9(x2+23x+109)=9(x2+2⋅13x+(13)2−(13)2+109)=9[(x+13)2+1]

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫3|3x+1|9x2+6x+10dx=∫1|x+13|9[1+(x+13)2]dx=13∫1|x+13|1+(x+13)2dx.

Let u=x+13. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

13∫1|x+13|1+(x+13)2dx=13∫1|u|1+u2du=−13arcsch⁡u+C=−13arcsch⁡(x+13)+C.

last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}9{x}^{2}+6x+10 & =9({x}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}x+\frac{10}{9}) \\  & =9({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{3}x+{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}+\frac{10}{9}) \\  & =9[{(x+\frac{1}{3})}^{2}+1]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

−13arcsch⁡(x+13)+C

EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

9x2+6x+10=9(x2+23x+109)=9(x2+2⋅13x+(13)2−(13)2+109)=9[(x+13)2+1]

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫3|3x+1|9x2+6x+10dx=∫1|x+13|9[1+(x+13)2]dx=13∫1|x+13|1+(x+13)2dx.

Let u=x+13. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

13∫1|x+13|1+(x+13)2dx=13∫1|u|1+u2du=−13arcsch⁡u+C=−13arcsch⁡(x+13)+C.

EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

9x2+6x+10=9(x2+23x+109)=9(x2+2⋅13x+(13)2−(13)2+109)=9[(x+13)2+1]

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫3|3x+1|9x2+6x+10dx=∫1|x+13|9[1+(x+13)2]dx=13∫1|x+13|1+(x+13)2dx.

Let u=x+13. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

13∫1|x+13|1+(x+13)2dx=13∫1|u|1+u2du=−13arcsch⁡u+C=−13arcsch⁡(x+13)+C.

question.name: Question 12
question.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+4x+5 & =4({x}^{2}+x+\frac{5}{4}) \\  & =4({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{5}{4}) \\  & =4[{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+1]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{|2x+1|\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+4x+5}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{2}|\sqrt{4[1+{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}]}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x+\frac{1}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x+\frac{1}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 12
?

∫2|2x+1|4x2+4x+5dx=

a
−12arcsch⁡(x+12)+C
b
−2arsech⁡(x+12)+C
c
−14arcsch⁡(x+12)+C
d
12arsech⁡(x+12)+C
e
−2arcsch⁡(x+12)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

4x2+4x+5=4(x2+x+54)=4(x2+2⋅12x+(12)2−(12)2+54)=4[(x+12)2+1]

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫2|2x+1|4x2+4x+5dx=∫1|x+12|4[1+(x+12)2]dx=12∫1|x+12|1+(x+12)2dx.

Let u=x+12. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

12∫1|x+12|1+(x+12)2dx=12∫1|u|1+u2du=−12arcsch⁡u+C=−12arcsch⁡(x+12)+C.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcosecant Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{x}^{2}+4x+5 & =4({x}^{2}+x+\frac{5}{4}) \\  & =4({x}^{2}+2\cdot \frac{1}{2}x+{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-{(\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+\frac{5}{4}) \\  & =4[{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+1]\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{|2x+1|\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+4x+5}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{2}|\sqrt{4[1+{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}]}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x+\frac{1}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x+\frac{1}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 12
?

∫2|2x+1|4x2+4x+5dx=

a
−12arcsch⁡(x+12)+C
b
−2arsech⁡(x+12)+C
c
−14arcsch⁡(x+12)+C
d
12arsech⁡(x+12)+C
e
−2arcsch⁡(x+12)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

4x2+4x+5=4(x2+x+54)=4(x2+2⋅12x+(12)2−(12)2+54)=4[(x+12)2+1]

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫2|2x+1|4x2+4x+5dx=∫1|x+12|4[1+(x+12)2]dx=12∫1|x+12|1+(x+12)2dx.

Let u=x+12. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

12∫1|x+12|1+(x+12)2dx=12∫1|u|1+u2du=−12arcsch⁡u+C=−12arcsch⁡(x+12)+C.

\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2}{|2x+1|\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+4x+5}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{2}|\sqrt{4[1+{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}]}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=x+\frac{1}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|x+\frac{1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(x+\frac{1}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x+\frac{1}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

4x2+4x+5=4(x2+x+54)=4(x2+2⋅12x+(12)2−(12)2+54)=4[(x+12)2+1]

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫2|2x+1|4x2+4x+5dx=∫1|x+12|4[1+(x+12)2]dx=12∫1|x+12|1+(x+12)2dx.

Let u=x+12. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

12∫1|x+12|1+(x+12)2dx=12∫1|u|1+u2du=−12arcsch⁡u+C=−12arcsch⁡(x+12)+C.

question.name: Question 13
question.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6x+13 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}+13 \\  & =(x+3)^{2}+4\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{6}{|x+3|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x+13}}\,\text{d}x & =-\int \frac{6}{|x+3|\sqrt{4+(x+3)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{6}{2|\frac{x+3}{2}|\sqrt{4+4{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+3}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+3}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+3}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =-\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =-3\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\frac{x+3}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

∫−6|x+3|x2+6x+13dx=

a
−3arsech⁡(x+32)+C
b
−32arsech⁡(x+32)+C
c
34arcsch⁡(x+32)+C
d
32arcsch⁡(x+32)+C
e
3arcsch⁡(x+32)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

x2+6x+13=x2+2⋅3x+32−32+13=(x+3)2+4

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫−6|x+3|x2+6x+13dx=−∫6|x+3|4+(x+3)2dx=−∫62|x+32|4+4(x+32)2dx=−32∫1|x+32|1+(x+32)2dx.

Let u=x+32. Then, we have dudx=12⟹dx=2du.

Therefore,

−32∫1|x+32|1+(x+32)2dx=−32∫1|u|1+u2⋅2du=−3∫1|u|1+u2du=3arcsch⁡u+C=3arcsch⁡(x+32)+C.

last_observation.name: Question 13
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcosecant Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6x+13 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}+13 \\  & =(x+3)^{2}+4\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{6}{|x+3|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x+13}}\,\text{d}x & =-\int \frac{6}{|x+3|\sqrt{4+(x+3)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{6}{2|\frac{x+3}{2}|\sqrt{4+4{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+3}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+3}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+3}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =-\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =-3\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\frac{x+3}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

b
−32arsech⁡(x+32)+C

EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

x2+6x+13=x2+2⋅3x+32−32+13=(x+3)2+4

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫−6|x+3|x2+6x+13dx=−∫6|x+3|4+(x+3)2dx=−∫62|x+32|4+4(x+32)2dx=−32∫1|x+32|1+(x+32)2dx.

Let u=x+32. Then, we have dudx=12⟹dx=2du.

Therefore,

−32∫1|x+32|1+(x+32)2dx=−32∫1|u|1+u2⋅2du=−3∫1|u|1+u2du=3arcsch⁡u+C=3arcsch⁡(x+32)+C.

solution.reasoning: Complete the square: x²+6x+13=(x+3)²+4. Set u=(x+3)/2, so dx=2 du. The integral becomes -3∫du/(|u|√(1+u²))=3 arcsch(u)+C, yielding option e. This holds for x≠-3, with independent constants on each interval. No Math Academy answer evidence for this question was captured.

feedback.name: Question 13
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+6x+13 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}+13 \\  & =(x+3)^{2}+4\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int -\frac{6}{|x+3|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+6x+13}}\,\text{d}x & =-\int \frac{6}{|x+3|\sqrt{4+(x+3)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\int \frac{6}{2|\frac{x+3}{2}|\sqrt{4+4{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+3}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+3}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}-\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+3}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+3}{2})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =-\frac{3}{2}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =-3\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =3\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\frac{x+3}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+5 & ={x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}+5 \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{2}{|4x-8|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-4x+5}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{2}{4|x-2|\sqrt{1+(x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|x-2|\sqrt{1+(x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|x-2|\sqrt{1+(x-2)^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x-2)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14
?

∫2|4x−8|x2−4x+5dx=

a
−12arsech⁡(x−2)+C
b
12arsech⁡(x−2)+C
c
−2arcsch⁡(x−2)+C
d
−12arcsch⁡(x−2)+C
e
2arsech⁡(x−2)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

x2−4x+5=x2−2⋅2x+22−22+5=(x−2)2+1

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫2|4x−8|x2−4x+5dx=∫24|x−2|1+(x−2)2dx=12∫1|x−2|1+(x−2)2dx.

Let u=x−2. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

12∫1|x−2|1+(x−2)2dx=12∫1|u|1+u2du=−12arcsch⁡u+C=−12arcsch⁡(x−2)+C.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcosecant Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-4x+5 & ={x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}+5 \\  & =(x-2)^{2}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{2}{|4x-8|\sqrt{{x}^{2}-4x+5}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{2}{4|x-2|\sqrt{1+(x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|x-2|\sqrt{1+(x-2)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=x-2.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|x-2|\sqrt{1+(x-2)^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(x-2)+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

x2−4x+5=x2−2⋅2x+22−22+5=(x−2)2+1

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫2|4x−8|x2−4x+5dx=∫24|x−2|1+(x−2)2dx=12∫1|x−2|1+(x−2)2dx.

Let u=x−2. Then, we have dudx=1⟹dx=du.

Therefore,

12∫1|x−2|1+(x−2)2dx=12∫1|u|1+u2du=−12arcsch⁡u+C=−12arcsch⁡(x−2)+C.

question.name: Question 15
question.problem: $\int \frac{4}{|x+1|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+2x+5}}\text{d}x=$
question.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x+5 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}+5 \\  & =(x+1)^{2}+4\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4}{|x+1|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+2x+5}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{4}{|x+1|\sqrt{4+(x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{2}{|\frac{x+1}{2}|\sqrt{4+4{(\frac{x+1}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+1}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+1}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+1}{2})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-2\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\frac{x+1}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

∫4|x+1|x2+2x+5dx=

a
−2arcsch⁡(x+12)+C
b
12arsech⁡(x+12)+C
c
−12arcsch⁡(x+12)+C
d
−4arcsch⁡(x+12)+C
e
2arsech⁡(x+12)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

x2+2x+5=x2+2⋅x+12−12+5=(x+1)2+4

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫4|x+1|x2+2x+5dx=∫4|x+1|4+(x+1)2dx=∫2|x+12|4+4(x+12)2dx=∫1|x+12|1+(x+12)2dx.

Let u=x+12. Then, we have dudx=12⟹dx=2du.

Therefore,

∫1|x+12|1+(x+12)2dx=∫1|u|1+u2⋅2du=2∫1|u|1+u2du=−2arcsch⁡u+C=−2arcsch⁡(x+12)+C.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcosecant Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+2x+5 & ={x}^{2}+2\cdot x+{1}^{2}-{1}^{2}+5 \\  & =(x+1)^{2}+4\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{4}{|x+1|\sqrt{{x}^{2}+2x+5}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{4}{|x+1|\sqrt{4+(x+1)^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{2}{|\frac{x+1}{2}|\sqrt{4+4{(\frac{x+1}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+1}{2})}^{2}}}\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $u=\frac{x+1}{2}.$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+1}{2})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-2\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\frac{x+1}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 15
?

∫4|x+1|x2+2x+5dx=

a
−2arcsch⁡(x+12)+C
b
12arsech⁡(x+12)+C
c
−12arcsch⁡(x+12)+C
d
−4arcsch⁡(x+12)+C
e
2arsech⁡(x+12)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the argument of the square root in the denominator:

x2+2x+5=x2+2⋅x+12−12+5=(x+1)2+4

Substituting the above into the given integral, we get ∫4|x+1|x2+2x+5dx=∫4|x+1|4+(x+1)2dx=∫2|x+12|4+4(x+12)2dx=∫1|x+12|1+(x+12)2dx.

Let u=x+12. Then, we have dudx=12⟹dx=2du.

Therefore,

∫1|x+12|1+(x+12)2dx=∫1|u|1+u2⋅2du=2∫1|u|1+u2du=−2arcsch⁡u+C=−2arcsch⁡(x+12)+C.

\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{|\frac{x+1}{2}|\sqrt{1+{(\frac{x+1}{2})}^{2}}}\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\int \frac{1}{|u|\sqrt{1+{u}^{2}}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-2\operatorname{arcsch}⁡u+C \\  & =-2\operatorname{arcsch}⁡(\frac{x+1}{2})+C.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 16
question.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-4x-{x}^{2} & =-({x}^{2}+4x-1) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}-1) \\  & =-((x+2)^{2}-5) \\  & =5-(x+2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-4x-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{5-(x+2)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2))+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{5}})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{5}}|>1.$

question.html:
Question 16
?

∫11−4x−x2dx=

a
15arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
b
−15arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
c
15arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
d
−55arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
e
55arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the denominator: 1−4x−x2=−(x2+4x−1)=−(x2+2⋅2x+22−22−1)=−((x+2)2−5)=5−(x+2)2

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get ∫11−4x−x2dx=∫15−(x+2)2dx=15∫11−(15(x+2))2dx.

Let u=15(x+2). Then, we have dudx=15⟹dx=5du.

Therefore, 15∫11−(15(x+2))2dx=15∫11−u2⋅5du=55∫11−u2du=55⋅arcoth⁡u+C=55⋅arcoth⁡(15(x+2))+C=55arcoth⁡(x+25)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x+25|>1.

last_observation.name: Question 16
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-4x-{x}^{2} & =-({x}^{2}+4x-1) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}-1) \\  & =-((x+2)^{2}-5) \\  & =5-(x+2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-4x-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{5-(x+2)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2))+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{5}})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{5}}|>1.$
