question.html:
Question 16
?

∫11−4x−x2dx=

a
15arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
b
−15arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
c
15arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
d
−55arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
e
55arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the denominator: 1−4x−x2=−(x2+4x−1)=−(x2+2⋅2x+22−22−1)=−((x+2)2−5)=5−(x+2)2

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get ∫11−4x−x2dx=∫15−(x+2)2dx=15∫11−(15(x+2))2dx.

Let u=15(x+2). Then, we have dudx=15⟹dx=5du.

Therefore, 15∫11−(15(x+2))2dx=15∫11−u2⋅5du=55∫11−u2du=55⋅arcoth⁡u+C=55⋅arcoth⁡(15(x+2))+C=55arcoth⁡(x+25)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x+25|>1.
question.knowledge_point: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral

solution.reasoning: Complete the square: 1-4x-x²=5-(x+2)². Set u=(x+2)/√5, so dx=√5 du. The integral becomes (√5/5)∫du/(1-u²)=(√5/5)arcoth(u)+C, giving option e for |x+2|>√5. On |x+2|<√5, use the corresponding artanh expression. No Math Academy answer evidence for this question was captured.

feedback.name: Question 16
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}1-4x-{x}^{2} & =-({x}^{2}+4x-1) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}-1) \\  & =-((x+2)^{2}-5) \\  & =5-(x+2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{1-4x-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{5-(x+2)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{5}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}(x+2))+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{5}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{5}})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x+2}{\sqrt{5}}|>1.$

Question 16

∫11−4x−x2dx=

a
15arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
b
−15arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
c
15arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
d
−55arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
e
55arcoth⁡(x+25)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the denominator: 1−4x−x2=−(x2+4x−1)=−(x2+2⋅2x+22−22−1)=−((x+2)2−5)=5−(x+2)2

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get ∫11−4x−x2dx=∫15−(x+2)2dx=15∫11−(15(x+2))2dx.

Let u=15(x+2). Then, we have dudx=15⟹dx=5du.

Therefore, 15∫11−(15(x+2))2dx=15∫11−u2⋅5du=55∫11−u2du=55⋅arcoth⁡u+C=55⋅arcoth⁡(15(x+2))+C=55arcoth⁡(x+25)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x+25|>1.

question.name: Question 17
question.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{9-(x+4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=$
question.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{1}{9-(x+4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{9-9(\frac{1}{9}(x+4)^{2})}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{3}(x+4))}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{3}(x+4).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{3}(x+4))}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{9}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+4}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x+4}{3}|>1.$

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{1}{9-(x+4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{9-9(\frac{1}{9}(x+4)^{2})}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{3}(x+4))}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{3}(x+4).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{3}(x+4))}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{9}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+4}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x+4}{3}|>1.$

question.html:
Question 17
?

Calculate ∫19−(x+4)2dx=

a
3arcoth⁡(x+43)+C
b
13arcoth⁡(x+43)+C
c
−19arcoth⁡(x+43)+C
d
−arcoth⁡(x+43)+C
e
13arcoth⁡(x+4)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we note that ∫19−(x+4)2dx=∫19−9(19(x+4)2)dx=19∫11−(13(x+4))2dx.

Let u=13(x+4). Then, we have

dudx=13⟹dx=3du.

Therefore,

19∫11−(13(x+4))2dx=19∫11−u2⋅3du=39⋅arcoth⁡u+C=13arcoth⁡(x+43)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x+43|>1.
question.knowledge_point: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral

solution.reasoning: Set u=(x+4)/3, so dx=3 du. The integral becomes (1/3)∫du/(1-u²)=(1/3)arcoth(u)+C, giving option b for |x+4|>3. On |x+4|<3, use (1/3)artanh(u)+C instead. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key for this question.

feedback.name: Question 17
feedback.problem: Calculate $\int \frac{1}{9-(x+4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=$
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we note that

$$
\int \frac{1}{9-(x+4)^{2}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{9-9(\frac{1}{9}(x+4)^{2})}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{3}(x+4))}^{2}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{3}(x+4).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{3}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=3\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{3}(x+4))}^{2}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{9}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\cdot 3\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{9}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{3}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x+4}{3})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x+4}{3}|>1.$

feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral

question.name: Question 18
question.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x-{x}^{2}-5 & =-({x}^{2}-6x+5) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}+5) \\  & =-((x-3)^{2}-4) \\  & =4-(x-3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{6x-{x}^{2}-5}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{4-(x-3)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{2}(x-3))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{2}(x-3).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{2}(x-3))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{2}(x-3))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x-3}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x-3}{2}|>1.$

question.html:
Question 18
?

∫16x−x2−5dx=

a
22arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
b
22arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
c
12arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
d
−22arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
e
−12arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the denominator: 6x−x2−5=−(x2−6x+5)=−(x2−2⋅3x+32−32+5)=−((x−3)2−4)=4−(x−3)2

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get ∫16x−x2−5dx=∫14−(x−3)2dx=14∫11−(12(x−3))2dx.

Let u=12(x−3). Then, we have dudx=12⟹dx=2du.

Therefore, 14∫11−(12(x−3))2dx=14∫11−u2⋅2du=12∫11−u2du=12⋅arcoth⁡u+C=12⋅arcoth⁡(12(x−3))+C=12arcoth⁡(x−32)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x−32|>1.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x-{x}^{2}-5 & =-({x}^{2}-6x+5) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}+5) \\  & =-((x-3)^{2}-4) \\  & =4-(x-3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{6x-{x}^{2}-5}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{4-(x-3)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{2}(x-3))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{2}(x-3).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{2}(x-3))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{2}(x-3))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x-3}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x-3}{2}|>1.$

question.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x-{x}^{2}-5 & =-({x}^{2}-6x+5) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}+5) \\  & =-((x-3)^{2}-4) \\  & =4-(x-3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{6x-{x}^{2}-5}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{4-(x-3)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{2}(x-3))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{2}(x-3).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{2}(x-3))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{2}(x-3))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x-3}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x-3}{2}|>1.$

Question 18
?

∫16x−x2−5dx=

a
22arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
b
22arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
c
12arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
d
−22arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
e
−12arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the denominator: 6x−x2−5=−(x2−6x+5)=−(x2−2⋅3x+32−32+5)=−((x−3)2−4)=4−(x−3)2

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get ∫16x−x2−5dx=∫14−(x−3)2dx=14∫11−(12(x−3))2dx.

Let u=12(x−3). Then, we have dudx=12⟹dx=2du.

Therefore, 14∫11−(12(x−3))2dx=14∫11−u2⋅2du=12∫11−u2du=12⋅arcoth⁡u+C=12⋅arcoth⁡(12(x−3))+C=12arcoth⁡(x−32)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x−32|>1.
question.knowledge_point: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral

solution.reasoning: Complete the square: 6x-x²-5=4-(x-3)². Set u=(x-3)/2, so dx=2 du. The integral becomes (1/2)∫du/(1-u²)=(1/2)arcoth(u)+C, giving option c for x<1 or x>5. On 1<x<5, use (1/2)artanh(u)+C. No Math Academy answer evidence for this question was captured.

feedback.name: Question 18
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}6x-{x}^{2}-5 & =-({x}^{2}-6x+5) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 3x+{3}^{2}-{3}^{2}+5) \\  & =-((x-3)^{2}-4) \\  & =4-(x-3)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{6x-{x}^{2}-5}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{4-(x-3)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{2}(x-3))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{2}(x-3).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{2}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=2\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{2}(x-3))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 2\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{2}(x-3))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x-3}{2})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x-3}{2}|>1.$

Question 18
?

∫16x−x2−5dx=

a
22arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
b
22arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
c
12arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
d
−22arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
e
−12arcoth⁡(x−32)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the denominator: 6x−x2−5=−(x2−6x+5)=−(x2−2⋅3x+32−32+5)=−((x−3)2−4)=4−(x−3)2

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get ∫16x−x2−5dx=∫14−(x−3)2dx=14∫11−(12(x−3))2dx.

Let u=12(x−3). Then, we have dudx=12⟹dx=2du.

Therefore, 14∫11−(12(x−3))2dx=14∫11−u2⋅2du=12∫11−u2du=12⋅arcoth⁡u+C=12⋅arcoth⁡(12(x−3))+C=12arcoth⁡(x−32)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x−32|>1.
feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral

question.name: Question 19
question.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}12x-{x}^{2}-33 & =-({x}^{2}-12x+33) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 6x+{6}^{2}-{6}^{2}+33) \\  & =-((x-6)^{2}-3) \\  & =3-(x-6)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{12x-{x}^{2}-33}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{3-(x-6)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6))+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x-6}{\sqrt{3}})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x-6}{\sqrt{3}}|>1.$

question.html:
Question 19
?

∫112x−x2−33dx=

a
13arcoth⁡(x−63)+C
b
33arcoth⁡(x−63)+C
c
−33arcoth⁡(x−63)+C
d
−13arcoth⁡(x−63)+C
e
13arcoth⁡(x−63)+C
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the denominator: 12x−x2−33=−(x2−12x+33)=−(x2−2⋅6x+62−62+33)=−((x−6)2−3)=3−(x−6)2

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get ∫112x−x2−33dx=∫13−(x−6)2dx=13∫11−(13(x−6))2dx.

Let u=13(x−6). Then, we have dudx=13⟹dx=3du.

Therefore, 13∫11−(13(x−6))2dx=13∫11−u2⋅3du=33∫11−u2du=33⋅arcoth⁡u+C=33⋅arcoth⁡(13(x−6))+C=33arcoth⁡(x−63)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x−63|>1.

last_observation.name: Question 19
last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}12x-{x}^{2}-33 & =-({x}^{2}-12x+33) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 6x+{6}^{2}-{6}^{2}+33) \\  & =-((x-6)^{2}-3) \\  & =3-(x-6)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{12x-{x}^{2}-33}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{3-(x-6)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6))+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x-6}{\sqrt{3}})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x-6}{\sqrt{3}}|>1.$

∫112x−x2−33dx=

a
13arcoth⁡(x−63)+C
b
33arcoth⁡(x−63)+C
c
−33arcoth⁡(x−63)+C
d
−13arcoth⁡(x−63)+C

13arcoth⁡(x−63)+C

EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the denominator: 12x−x2−33=−(x2−12x+33)=−(x2−2⋅6x+62−62+33)=−((x−6)2−3)=3−(x−6)2

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get ∫112x−x2−33dx=∫13−(x−6)2dx=13∫11−(13(x−6))2dx.

Let u=13(x−6). Then, we have dudx=13⟹dx=3du.

Therefore, 13∫11−(13(x−6))2dx=13∫11−u2⋅3du=33∫11−u2du=33⋅arcoth⁡u+C=33⋅arcoth⁡(13(x−6))+C=33arcoth⁡(x−63)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x−63|>1.
question.knowledge_point: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral

solution.reasoning: Complete the square: 12x-x²-33=3-(x-6)². Set u=(x-6)/√3, so dx=√3 du. The integral becomes (√3/3)∫du/(1-u²)=(√3/3)arcoth(u)+C, giving option b for |x-6|>√3. On |x-6|<√3, use the corresponding artanh expression. No Math Academy answer evidence for this question was captured.

feedback.name: Question 19
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}12x-{x}^{2}-33 & =-({x}^{2}-12x+33) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 6x+{6}^{2}-{6}^{2}+33) \\  & =-((x-6)^{2}-3) \\  & =3-(x-6)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{12x-{x}^{2}-33}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{3-(x-6)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(x-6))+C \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{3}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x-6}{\sqrt{3}})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x-6}{\sqrt{3}}|>1.$

feedback.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral

question.name: Question 20
question.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}12+4x-{x}^{2} & =-({x}^{2}-4x-12) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}-12) \\  & =-((x-2)^{2}-16) \\  & =16-(x-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{12+4x-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{16-(x-2)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{4}(x-2))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{4}(x-2).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{4}(x-2))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 4\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{4}(x-2))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x-2}{4})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x-2}{4}|>1.$

question.html:
Question 20
?

∫112+4x−x2dx=

a
18arcoth⁡(x−24)+C
b
14arcoth⁡(x−22)+C
c
14arcoth⁡(x−24)+C
d
116arcoth⁡(x−24)+C
e
−116arcoth⁡(x−22)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the denominator: 12+4x−x2=−(x2−4x−12)=−(x2−2⋅2x+22−22−12)=−((x−2)2−16)=16−(x−2)2

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get ∫112+4x−x2dx=∫116−(x−2)2dx=116∫11−(14(x−2))2dx.

Let u=14(x−2). Then, we have dudx=14⟹dx=4du.

Therefore, 116∫11−(14(x−2))2dx=116∫11−u2⋅4du=14∫11−u2du=14⋅arcoth⁡u+C=14⋅arcoth⁡(14(x−2))+C=14arcoth⁡(x−24)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x−24|>1.

last_observation.knowledge_point: Example: Completing the Square to Compute a Hyperbolic Arcotangent Integral
last_observation.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}12+4x-{x}^{2} & =-({x}^{2}-4x-12) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}-12) \\  & =-((x-2)^{2}-16) \\  & =16-(x-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{12+4x-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{16-(x-2)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{4}(x-2))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{4}(x-2).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{4}(x-2))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 4\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{4}(x-2))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x-2}{4})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x-2}{4}|>1.$

∫112+4x−x2dx=

a
18arcoth⁡(x−24)+C
b
14arcoth⁡(x−22)+C
c
14arcoth⁡(x−24)+C
d
116arcoth⁡(x−24)+C
e
−116arcoth⁡(x−22)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the denominator: 12+4x−x2=−(x2−4x−12)=−(x2−2⋅2x+22−22−12)=−((x−2)2−16)=16−(x−2)2

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get ∫112+4x−x2dx=∫116−(x−2)2dx=116∫11−(14(x−2))2dx.

Let u=14(x−2). Then, we have dudx=14⟹dx=4du.

Therefore, 116∫11−(14(x−2))2dx=116∫11−u2⋅4du=14∫11−u2du=14⋅arcoth⁡u+C=14⋅arcoth⁡(14(x−2))+C=14arcoth⁡(x−24)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x−24|>1.

solution.reasoning: Complete the square: 12+4x-x²=16-(x-2)². Set u=(x-2)/4, so dx=4 du. The integral becomes (1/4)∫du/(1-u²)=(1/4)arcoth(u)+C, giving option c for x<-2 or x>6. On -2<x<6, use the corresponding artanh expression. No Math Academy answer evidence for this question was captured.

feedback.name: Question 20
feedback.worked_solution:
First, we complete the square for the denominator:

$$
\begin{aligned}12+4x-{x}^{2} & =-({x}^{2}-4x-12) \\  & =-({x}^{2}-2\cdot 2x+{2}^{2}-{2}^{2}-12) \\  & =-((x-2)^{2}-16) \\  & =16-(x-2)^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get

$$
\int \frac{1}{12+4x-{x}^{2}}\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{16-(x-2)^{2}}\text{d}x=\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{4}(x-2))}^{2}}\text{d}x.
$$

Let $u=\frac{1}{4}(x-2).$ Then, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{4}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=4\,\text{d}u.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{(\frac{1}{4}(x-2))}^{2}}\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{16}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\cdot 4\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\int \frac{1}{1-{u}^{2}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\cdot \operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{1}{4}(x-2))+C \\  & =\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{arcoth}⁡(\frac{x-2}{4})+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that this result is subject to the condition $|\frac{x-2}{4}|>1.$

feedback.html:
Question 20
?

∫112+4x−x2dx=

a
18arcoth⁡(x−24)+C
b
14arcoth⁡(x−22)+C
c
14arcoth⁡(x−24)+C
d
116arcoth⁡(x−24)+C
e
−116arcoth⁡(x−22)+C
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, we complete the square for the denominator: 12+4x−x2=−(x2−4x−12)=−(x2−2⋅2x+22−22−12)=−((x−2)2−16)=16−(x−2)2

Substituting the above into the denominator of our integral, we get ∫112+4x−x2dx=∫116−(x−2)2dx=116∫11−(14(x−2))2dx.

Let u=14(x−2). Then, we have dudx=14⟹dx=4du.

Therefore, 116∫11−(14(x−2))2dx=116∫11−u2⋅4du=14∫11−u2du=14⋅arcoth⁡u+C=14⋅arcoth⁡(14(x−2))+C=14arcoth⁡(x−24)+C.

Note that this result is subject to the condition |x−24|>1.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Consider the function $f:{R}^{3}\to R$ defined by $f(x)={x}^{T}x.$ What is the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $x?$
questions.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a scalar-valued function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ with respect to a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ is the row vector

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{1\times n}.
$$

In our case, the function 

- acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{3},$ and

- outputs a scalar $f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3})\in R$ defined by 

$$
f(x)={x}^{T}x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2} & {x}_{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1} & 2{x}_{2} & 2{x}_{3}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{1\times 3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can also write this as

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=2{x}^{T}.
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Consider the function $f,$ defined as 

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} \\ x\end{aligned}].
$$

What is the shape of the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $x?$
questions.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a vector-valued function $f:R\to {R}^{m}$ with respect to a scalar $x$ is the column vector

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} \\ ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂x}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{m\times 1}.
$$

In our case, the function 

- acts on a scalar $x\in R,$ and

- outputs a vector $f(x)\in {R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the total derivative will be a column vector of shape $2\times 1.$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Consider the function $f:R\to {R}^{4},$ defined by 

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 4 & -5 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

What is the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $x?$
questions.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a vector-valued function $f:R\to {R}^{m}$ with respect to a scalar $x$ is the column vector

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} \\ ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂x}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{m\times 1}.
$$

In our case, the function 

- acts on a scalar $x\in R,$ and

- outputs a vector $f(x)\in {R}^{4}$ defined by 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 4 & -5 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}x+2 \\ 3x \\ 4x-10 \\ 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{4}}{∂x}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+2) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(3x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-10) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(6)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{4\times 1}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Consider the vector-valued function $f:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ defined by

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]x.
$$

 

What is $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x},$ the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a vector-valued function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ with respect to a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ is the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{m\times n}.
$$

In our case, writing out the function $f(x)$ where $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{3}$, we get

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the total derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Since the total derivative is a constant matrix, evaluating it at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ gives the same matrix.

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a scalar-valued function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ with respect to a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ is the row vector

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{1\times n}.
$$

In our case, the function 

- acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{3},$ and

- outputs a scalar $f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3})\in R$ defined by 

$$
f(x)={x}^{T}x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2} & {x}_{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1} & 2{x}_{2} & 2{x}_{3}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{1\times 3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can also write this as

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=2{x}^{T}.
$$

$$

In our case, the function 

- acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{3},$ and

- outputs a scalar $f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3})\in R$ defined by 

$$
f(x)={x}^{T}x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2} & {x}_{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}.

Question 1

Consider the function f:R3→R defined by f(x)=xTx. What is the total derivative of f with respect to x?

a
2xT

x

xxT

2x

xTx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The total derivative of a scalar-valued function f:Rn→R with respect to a vector x∈Rn is the row vector dfdx=[∂f∂x1∂f∂x2⋯∂f∂xn]∈R1×n.

In our case, the function

  • acts on a vector x∈R3, and

  • outputs a scalar f(x1,x2,x3)∈R defined by f(x)=xTx=[x1x2x3][x1x2x3]=x12+x22+x32.

Therefore, we have
dfdx=[∂f∂x1∂f∂x2∂f∂x3]=[∂∂x1(x12+x22+x32)∂∂x2(x12+x22+x32)∂∂x3(x12+x22+x32)]=[2x12x22x3]∈R1×3.

We can also write this as dfdx=2xT.

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a vector-valued function $f:R\to {R}^{m}$ with respect to a scalar $x$ is the column vector

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} \\ ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂x}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{m\times 1}.
$$

In our case, the function 

- acts on a scalar $x\in R,$ and

- outputs a vector $f(x)\in {R}^{4}$ defined by 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 4 & -5 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}x+2 \\ 3x \\ 4x-10 \\ 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{4}}{∂x}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+2) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(3x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-10) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(6)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{4\times 1}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 3
?

Consider the function f:R→R4, defined by f(x)=[11304−503]⋅[x2].

What is the total derivative of f with respect to x?

a
[10−53]
b
[1340]
c
[x3x−5x1]
d
[1340]
e
[10−53]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The total derivative of a vector-valued function f:R→Rm with respect to a scalar x is the column vector

dfdx=[∂f1∂x∂f2∂x⋮∂fm∂x]∈Rm×1.

In our case, the function

  • acts on a scalar x∈R, and

  • outputs a vector f(x)∈R4 defined by f(x)=[11304−503]⋅[x2]=[x+23x4x−106].

Therefore, we have
dfdx=[∂f1∂x∂f2∂x∂f3∂x∂f4∂x]=[∂∂x(x+2)∂∂x(3x)∂∂x(4x−10)∂∂x(6)]=[1340]∈R4×1.

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a vector-valued function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ with respect to a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ is the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{m\times n}.
$$

In our case, writing out the function $f(x)$ where $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{3}$, we get

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the total derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Since the total derivative is a constant matrix, evaluating it at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ gives the same matrix.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Consider the vector-valued function $f:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ defined by

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]x.
$$

 

What is $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x},$ the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]?$
question.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a vector-valued function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ with respect to a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ is the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{m\times n}.
$$

In our case, writing out the function $f(x)$ where $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{3}$, we get

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the total derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Since the total derivative is a constant matrix, evaluating it at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ gives the same matrix.

Question 4
?

Consider the vector-valued function f:R3→R3 defined by f(x)=[110101011]x.

What is dfdx, the total derivative of f with respect to x at x0=[102]?

a
[101011110]
b
[1110]
c
[100010001]
d
[110101011]
e
[100101001]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The total derivative of a vector-valued function f:Rn→Rm with respect to a vector x∈Rn is the m×n matrix dfdx=[∂f1∂x1∂f1∂x2⋯∂f1∂xn∂f2∂x1∂f2∂x2⋯∂f2∂xn⋮⋮⋱⋮∂fm∂x1∂fm∂x2⋯∂fm∂xn]∈Rm×n.

In our case, writing out the function f(x) where x=[x1x2x3]∈R3, we get f(x)=[110101011][x1x2x3]=[x1+x2x1+x3x2+x3].

So, the total derivative is dfdx=[∂f1∂x1∂f1∂x2∂f1∂x3∂f2∂x1∂f2∂x2∂f2∂x3∂f3∂x1∂f3∂x2∂f3∂x3]=[∂∂x1(x1+x2)∂∂x2(x1+x2)∂∂x3(x1+x2)∂∂x1(x1+x3)∂∂x2(x1+x3)∂∂x3(x1+x3)∂∂x1(x2+x3)∂∂x2(x2+x3)∂∂x3(x2+x3)]=[110101011].

Since the total derivative is a constant matrix, evaluating it at x0=[102] gives the same matrix.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Consider the function $f:{R}^{3}\to R$ defined by $f(x)={x}^{T}x.$ What is the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $x?$
question.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a scalar-valued function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ with respect to a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ is the row vector

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{1\times n}.
$$

In our case, the function 

- acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{3},$ and

- outputs a scalar $f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3})\in R$ defined by 

$$
f(x)={x}^{T}x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2} & {x}_{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1} & 2{x}_{2} & 2{x}_{3}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{1\times 3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can also write this as

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=2{x}^{T}.

Question 1

Consider the function f:R3→R defined by f(x)=xTx. What is the total derivative of f with respect to x?

a
2xT
b
x
c
xxT
d
2x
e
xTx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The total derivative of a scalar-valued function f:Rn→R with respect to a vector x∈Rn is the row vector dfdx=[∂f∂x1∂f∂x2⋯∂f∂xn]∈R1×n.

In our case, the function

  • acts on a vector x∈R3, and

  • outputs a scalar f(x1,x2,x3)∈R defined by f(x)=xTx=[x1x2x3][x1x2x3]=x12+x22+x32.

Therefore, we have
dfdx=[∂f∂x1∂f∂x2∂f∂x3]=[∂∂x1(x12+x22+x32)∂∂x2(x12+x22+x32)∂∂x3(x12+x22+x32)]=[2x12x22x3]∈R1×3.

We can also write this as dfdx=2xT.

last_observation.name: Question 1
last_observation.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a scalar-valued function $f:{R}^{n}\to R$ with respect to a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ is the row vector

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{1\times n}.
$$

In our case, the function 

- acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{3},$ and

- outputs a scalar $f({x}_{1},{x}_{2},{x}_{3})\in R$ defined by 

$$
f(x)={x}^{T}x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} & {x}_{2} & {x}_{3}\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]={x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂f}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2{x}_{1} & 2{x}_{2} & 2{x}_{3}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{1\times 3}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can also write this as

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=2{x}^{T}.
$$

Question 1
?

Consider the function f:R3→R defined by f(x)=xTx. What is the total derivative of f with respect to x?

a
2xT
b
x
c
xxT
d
2x
e
xTx
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The total derivative of a scalar-valued function f:Rn→R with respect to a vector x∈Rn is the row vector dfdx=[∂f∂x1∂f∂x2⋯∂f∂xn]∈R1×n.

In our case, the function

  • acts on a vector x∈R3, and

  • outputs a scalar f(x1,x2,x3)∈R defined by f(x)=xTx=[x1x2x3][x1x2x3]=x12+x22+x32.

Therefore, we have
dfdx=[∂f∂x1∂f∂x2∂f∂x3]=[∂∂x1(x12+x22+x32)∂∂x2(x12+x22+x32)∂∂x3(x12+x22+x32)]=[2x12x22x3]∈R1×3.

We can also write this as dfdx=2xT.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem:
Consider the function $f,$ defined as 

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2} \\ x\end{aligned}].
$$

What is the shape of the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $x?$
question.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a vector-valued function $f:R\to {R}^{m}$ with respect to a scalar $x$ is the column vector

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} \\ ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂x}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{m\times 1}.
$$

In our case, the function 

- acts on a scalar $x\in R,$ and

- outputs a vector $f(x)\in {R}^{2}.$

Therefore, the total derivative will be a column vector of shape $2\times 1.$

- outputs a vector $f(x)\in {R}^{4}$ defined by 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 4 & -5 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}x+2 \\ 3x \\ 4x-10 \\ 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{4}}{∂x}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+2) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(3x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-10) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(6)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{4\times 1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Consider the function f:R→R4, defined by f(x)=[11304−503]⋅[x2].

What is the total derivative of f with respect to x?

a
[10−53]
b
[1340]
c
[x3x−5x1]
d
[1340]
e
[10−53]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The total derivative of a vector-valued function f:R→Rm with respect to a scalar x is the column vector

dfdx=[∂f1∂x∂f2∂x⋮∂fm∂x]∈Rm×1.

In our case, the function

  • acts on a scalar x∈R, and

  • outputs a vector f(x)∈R4 defined by f(x)=[11304−503]⋅[x2]=[x+23x4x−106].

Therefore, we have
dfdx=[∂f1∂x∂f2∂x∂f3∂x∂f4∂x]=[∂∂x(x+2)∂∂x(3x)∂∂x(4x−10)∂∂x(6)]=[1340]∈R4×1.

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a vector-valued function $f:R\to {R}^{m}$ with respect to a scalar $x$ is the column vector

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} \\ ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂x}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{m\times 1}.
$$

In our case, the function 

- acts on a scalar $x\in R,$ and

- outputs a vector $f(x)\in {R}^{4}$ defined by 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 4 & -5 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}x+2 \\ 3x \\ 4x-10 \\ 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{4}}{∂x}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+2) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(3x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-10) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(6)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{4\times 1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Consider the function f:R→R4, defined by f(x)=[11304−503]⋅[x2].

What is the total derivative of f with respect to x?

a
[10−53]
b
[1340]
c
[x3x−5x1]
d
[1340]
e
[10−53]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The total derivative of a vector-valued function f:R→Rm with respect to a scalar x is the column vector

dfdx=[∂f1∂x∂f2∂x⋮∂fm∂x]∈Rm×1.

In our case, the function

  • acts on a scalar x∈R, and

  • outputs a vector f(x)∈R4 defined by f(x)=[11304−503]⋅[x2]=[x+23x4x−106].

Therefore, we have
dfdx=[∂f1∂x∂f2∂x∂f3∂x∂f4∂x]=[∂∂x(x+2)∂∂x(3x)∂∂x(4x−10)∂∂x(6)]=[1340]∈R4×1.

solution.reasoning: Multiplication gives f(x)=(x+2,3x,4x-10,6)^T. Differentiating each component gives Df(x)=(1,3,4,0)^T, a 4-by-1 column vector. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.problem:

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 4 & -5 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x \\ 2\end{aligned}].

What is the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $x?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a vector-valued function $f:R\to {R}^{m}$ with respect to a scalar $x$ is the column vector

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} \\ ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂x}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{m\times 1}.
$$

In our case, the function 

- acts on a scalar $x\in R,$ and

- outputs a vector $f(x)\in {R}^{4}$ defined by 

$$
\begin{aligned}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 3 & 0 \\ 4 & -5 \\ 0 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}x \\ 2\end{aligned}] & =[\begin{aligned}x+2 \\ 3x \\ 4x-10 \\ 6\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂x} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{4}}{∂x}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+2) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(3x) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(4x-10) \\ \frac{∂}{∂x}(6)\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3 \\ 4 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{4\times 1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Consider the function f:R→R4, defined by f(x)=[11304−503]⋅[x2].

What is the total derivative of f with respect to x?

a
[10−53]
b
[1340]
c
[x3x−5x1]
d
[1340]
e
[10−53]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The total derivative of a vector-valued function f:R→Rm with respect to a scalar x is the column vector

dfdx=[∂f1∂x∂f2∂x⋮∂fm∂x]∈Rm×1.

In our case, the function

  • acts on a scalar x∈R, and

  • outputs a vector f(x)∈R4 defined by f(x)=[11304−503]⋅[x2]=[x+23x4x−106].

Therefore, we have
dfdx=[∂f1∂x∂f2∂x∂f3∂x∂f4∂x]=[∂∂x(x+2)∂∂x(3x)∂∂x(4x−10)∂∂x(6)]=[1340]∈R4×1.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Consider the vector-valued function $f:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ defined by

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]x.
$$

 

What is $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x},$ the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]?$
question.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a vector-valued function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ with respect to a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ is the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{m\times n}.
$$

In our case, writing out the function $f(x)$ where $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{3}$, we get

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the total derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Since the total derivative is a constant matrix, evaluating it at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ gives the same matrix.

question.html:
Question 4
?

Consider the vector-valued function f:R3→R3 defined by f(x)=[110101011]x.

What is dfdx, the total derivative of f with respect to x at x0=[102]?

a
[101011110]
b
[1110]
c
[100010001]
d
[110101011]
e
[100101001]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The total derivative of a vector-valued function f:Rn→Rm with respect to a vector x∈Rn is the m×n matrix dfdx=[∂f1∂x1∂f1∂x2⋯∂f1∂xn∂f2∂x1∂f2∂x2⋯∂f2∂xn⋮⋮⋱⋮∂fm∂x1∂fm∂x2⋯∂fm∂xn]∈Rm×n.

In our case, writing out the function f(x) where x=[x1x2x3]∈R3, we get f(x)=[110101011][x1x2x3]=[x1+x2x1+x3x2+x3].

So, the total derivative is dfdx=[∂f1∂x1∂f1∂x2∂f1∂x3∂f2∂x1∂f2∂x2∂f2∂x3∂f3∂x1∂f3∂x2∂f3∂x3]=[∂∂x1(x1+x2)∂∂x2(x1+x2)∂∂x3(x1+x2)∂∂x1(x1+x3)∂∂x2(x1+x3)∂∂x3(x1+x3)∂∂x1(x2+x3)∂∂x2(x2+x3)∂∂x3(x2+x3)]=[110101011].

Since the total derivative is a constant matrix, evaluating it at x0=[102] gives the same matrix.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a vector-valued function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ with respect to a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ is the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{m\times n}.
$$

In our case, writing out the function $f(x)$ where $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{3}$, we get

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the total derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Since the total derivative is a constant matrix, evaluating it at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ gives the same matrix.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem:
Consider the vector-valued function $f:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ defined by

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]x.
$$

 

What is $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x},$ the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]?$
question.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a vector-valued function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ with respect to a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ is the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{m\times n}.
$$

In our case, writing out the function $f(x)$ where $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{3}$, we get

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the total derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Since the total derivative is a constant matrix, evaluating it at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ gives the same matrix.

question.html:
Question 4
?

Consider the vector-valued function f:R3→R3 defined by f(x)=[110101011]x.

What is dfdx, the total derivative of f with respect to x at x0=[102]?

a
[101011110]
b
[1110]
c
[100010001]
d
[110101011]
e
[100101001]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The total derivative of a vector-valued function f:Rn→Rm with respect to a vector x∈Rn is the m×n matrix dfdx=[∂f1∂x1∂f1∂x2⋯∂f1∂xn∂f2∂x1∂f2∂x2⋯∂f2∂xn⋮⋮⋱⋮∂fm∂x1∂fm∂x2⋯∂fm∂xn]∈Rm×n.

In our case, writing out the function f(x) where x=[x1x2x3]∈R3, we get f(x)=[110101011][x1x2x3]=[x1+x2x1+x3x2+x3].

So, the total derivative is dfdx=[∂f1∂x1∂f1∂x2∂f1∂x3∂f2∂x1∂f2∂x2∂f2∂x3∂f3∂x1∂f3∂x2∂f3∂x3]=[∂∂x1(x1+x2)∂∂x2(x1+x2)∂∂x3(x1+x2)∂∂x1(x1+x3)∂∂x2(x1+x3)∂∂x3(x1+x3)∂∂x1(x2+x3)∂∂x2(x2+x3)∂∂x3(x2+x3)]=[110101011].

Since the total derivative is a constant matrix, evaluating it at x0=[102] gives the same matrix.

solution.reasoning: For a linear function f(x)=Ax, f(x+h)-f(x)=Ah exactly, so Df(x)=A at every point, including x₀. Thus option d is mathematically correct. No captured Math Academy answer or grade establishes its key.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem:
Consider the vector-valued function $f:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{3}$ defined by

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]x.
$$

 

What is $\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x},$ the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $x$ at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The total derivative of a vector-valued function $f:{R}^{n}\to {R}^{m}$ with respect to a vector $x\in {R}^{n}$ is the $m\times n$ matrix

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{n}} \\ ⋮ & ⋮ & ⋱ & ⋮ \\ \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{2}} & ⋯ & \frac{∂{f}_{m}}{∂{x}_{n}}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{m\times n}.
$$

In our case, writing out the function $f(x)$ where $x=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]\in {R}^{3}$, we get

$$
f(x)=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ {x}_{2} \\ {x}_{3}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}+{x}_{2} \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{2}+{x}_{3}\end{aligned}].
$$

So, the total derivative is

$$
\begin{aligned}\,\,\,\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{2}+{x}_{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Since the total derivative is a constant matrix, evaluating it at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 2\end{aligned}]$ gives the same matrix.

Question 4
?

Consider the vector-valued function f:R3→R3 defined by f(x)=[110101011]x.

What is dfdx, the total derivative of f with respect to x at x0=[102]?

a
[101011110]
b
[1110]
c
[100010001]
d
[110101011]
e
[100101001]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The total derivative of a vector-valued function f:Rn→Rm with respect to a vector x∈Rn is the m×n matrix dfdx=[∂f1∂x1∂f1∂x2⋯∂f1∂xn∂f2∂x1∂f2∂x2⋯∂f2∂xn⋮⋮⋱⋮∂fm∂x1∂fm∂x2⋯∂fm∂xn]∈Rm×n.

In our case, writing out the function f(x) where x=[x1x2x3]∈R3, we get f(x)=[110101011][x1x2x3]=[x1+x2x1+x3x2+x3].

So, the total derivative is dfdx=[∂f1∂x1∂f1∂x2∂f1∂x3∂f2∂x1∂f2∂x2∂f2∂x3∂f3∂x1∂f3∂x2∂f3∂x3]=[∂∂x1(x1+x2)∂∂x2(x1+x2)∂∂x3(x1+x2)∂∂x1(x1+x3)∂∂x2(x1+x3)∂∂x3(x1+x3)∂∂x1(x2+x3)∂∂x2(x2+x3)∂∂x3(x2+x3)]=[110101011].

Since the total derivative is a constant matrix, evaluating it at x0=[102] gives the same matrix.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ?$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \pi .$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\sqrt{2}$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}?$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{2})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{2})^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=2$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}?$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(2)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}x(1-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=1\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{8}?$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{8}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x(1-{y}^{2})$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+0} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x(1-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le -\frac{\pi }{8}?$
questions.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le -\frac{\pi }{8}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }{{(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )=-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta },\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }+\frac{1}{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Reducing the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve to a Definite Integral
questions.raw_html:
5.Reducing the Line Integral of a Scalar Function Along a Curve to a Definite Integral?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cy4x2ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=cot⁡θ for −π4≤θ≤−π8?

E
Wed, Oct 14th @ 10:05 PM|Elapsed: 0:16Correct

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \pi .$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \pi .$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫C(x2+y2)ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=2sin⁡θ for 0≤θ≤π?

a
2∫0πsin⁡θdθ
b
4∫0πcos2⁡θdθ
c
2∫0πsin2⁡θdθ
d
8∫0πcos⁡θdθ
e
8∫0πsin2⁡θdθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=2sin⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=2sin⁡θcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=2sin2⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=2sin⁡θcos⁡θ and y=2sin2⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π.

Now, if f(x,y)=x2+y2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=(2sin⁡θcos⁡θ)2+(2sin2⁡θ)2=4sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+4sin4⁡θ=4sin2⁡θ(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=4sin2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2sin⁡θ)=2cos⁡θ,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(2sin⁡θ)2+(2cos⁡θ)2=4sin2⁡θ+4cos2⁡θ=4(sin2⁡θ+cos2⁡θ)=2.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫C(x2+y2)ds=∫0πf(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π4sin2⁡θ⋅2⋅dθ=8∫0πsin2⁡θdθ.

observed_steps.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{2})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{2})^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cx2yds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=2 for −π4≤θ≤π4?

a
4∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ
b
4∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos⁡θdθ
c
22∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos⁡θdθ
d
2∫−π/4π/4sin2⁡θcos⁡θdθ
e
2∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=2cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=2cos⁡θ and y=2sin⁡θ, where −π4≤θ≤π4.

Now, if f(x,y)=x2y, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=(2cos⁡θ)2⋅2sin⁡θ=22sin⁡θcos2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(2)2+02=2.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cx2yds=∫−π/4π/4f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/4π/422sin⁡θcos2⁡θ⋅2⋅dθ=4∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ.

observed_steps.name: Question 3
observed_steps.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(2)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(2)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$
