question.html:
Question 3
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cxy2ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=2 for 0≤θ≤π4?

a
32∫0π/4(sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ)2dθ
b
8∫0π/4sin2⁡θcos4⁡θdθ
c
8∫0π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ
d
4∫0π/4(sin⁡θ+cos2⁡θ)dθ
e
16∫0π/4cos⁡θsin2⁡θdθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=2cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=2cos⁡θ and y=2sin⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π4.

Now, if f(x,y)=xy2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=2cos⁡θ⋅(2sin⁡θ)2=8cos⁡θsin2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(2)2+02=2.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cxy2ds=∫0π/4f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/48cos⁡θsin2⁡θ⋅2⋅dθ=16∫0π/4cos⁡θsin2⁡θdθ.

observed_steps.name: Question 4
observed_steps.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{8}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x(1-{y}^{2})$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+0} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x(1-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{8}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x(1-{y}^{2})$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+0} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x(1-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cx(1−y2)ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=1 for 0≤θ≤π8?

a
∫0π/8cos2⁡θsin2⁡θdθ
b
2∫0π/8sin2⁡θdθ
c
∫0π/8cos3⁡θdθ
d
2∫0π/8cos2⁡θdθ
e
4∫0π/8cos2⁡θsin⁡θdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=1⋅cos⁡θ=cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=1⋅sin⁡θ=sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=cos⁡θ and y=sin⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π8.

Now, if f(x,y)=x(1−y2), we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=cos⁡θ(1−sin2⁡θ)=cos⁡θ⋅cos2⁡θ=cos3⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(1)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=12+02=1+0=1.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cx(1−y2)ds=∫0π/8f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/8cos3⁡θ⋅1⋅dθ=∫0π/8cos3⁡θdθ.

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le -\frac{\pi }{8}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }{{(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )=-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta },\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }+\frac{1}{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le -\frac{\pi }{8}?$

\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le -\frac{\pi }{8}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }{{(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )=-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta },\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }+\frac{1}{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cy4x2ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=cot⁡θ for −π4≤θ≤−π8?

a
∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
b
∫−π/4−π/8cos2⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
c
∫−π/4−π/8sin⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
d
∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
e
∫−π/4−π/8cos⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rsin⁡θ=cot⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=cos⁡θsin⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=cos2⁡θsin⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=cot⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=cos⁡θsin⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=cos⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=cos2⁡θsin⁡θ and y=cos⁡θ, where −π4≤θ≤−π8.

Now, if f(x,y)=y4x2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=cos4⁡θ(cos2⁡θsin⁡θ)2=sin2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(cot⁡θ)=−1sin2⁡θ,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(cot⁡θ)2+(−1sin2⁡θ)2=cos2⁡θsin2⁡θ+1sin4⁡θ=sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1sin4⁡θ=sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1sin2⁡θ.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cy4x2ds=∫−π/4−π/8f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θ⋅sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1sin2⁡θdθ=∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ.

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ?$
question.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \pi .$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫C(x2+y2)ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=2sin⁡θ for 0≤θ≤π?

a
2∫0πsin⁡θdθ
b
4∫0πcos2⁡θdθ
c
2∫0πsin2⁡θdθ
d
8∫0πcos⁡θdθ
e
8∫0πsin2⁡θdθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=2sin⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=2sin⁡θcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=2sin2⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=2sin⁡θcos⁡θ and y=2sin2⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π.

Now, if f(x,y)=x2+y2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=(2sin⁡θcos⁡θ)2+(2sin2⁡θ)2=4sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+4sin4⁡θ=4sin2⁡θ(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=4sin2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2sin⁡θ)=2cos⁡θ,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(2sin⁡θ)2+(2cos⁡θ)2=4sin2⁡θ+4cos2⁡θ=4(sin2⁡θ+cos2⁡θ)=2.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫C(x2+y2)ds=∫0πf(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π4sin2⁡θ⋅2⋅dθ=8∫0πsin2⁡θdθ.

last_observation.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \pi .$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫C(x2+y2)ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=2sin⁡θ for 0≤θ≤π?

a
2∫0πsin⁡θdθ
b
4∫0πcos2⁡θdθ
c
2∫0πsin2⁡θdθ
d
8∫0πcos⁡θdθ
e
8∫0πsin2⁡θdθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=2sin⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=2sin⁡θcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=2sin2⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=2sin⁡θcos⁡θ and y=2sin2⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π.

Now, if f(x,y)=x2+y2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=(2sin⁡θcos⁡θ)2+(2sin2⁡θ)2=4sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+4sin4⁡θ=4sin2⁡θ(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=4sin2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2sin⁡θ)=2cos⁡θ,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(2sin⁡θ)2+(2cos⁡θ)2=4sin2⁡θ+4cos2⁡θ=4(sin2⁡θ+cos2⁡θ)=2.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫C(x2+y2)ds=∫0πf(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π4sin2⁡θ⋅2⋅dθ=8∫0πsin2⁡θdθ.

solution.reasoning: Since x²+y²=r²=4sin²θ and ds=√(r²+(dr/dθ)²)dθ=√(4sin²θ+4cos²θ)dθ=2dθ, the integral equals 8∫₀^π sin²θ dθ, which is option e. No captured Math Academy answer or grading evidence establishes its stated key.

feedback.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,$ for $0\le \theta \le \pi ?$
feedback.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \pi .$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & ={(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}^{2} \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +4{sin}^{4}⁡\theta  \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta } \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡\theta +{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }4{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫C(x2+y2)ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=2sin⁡θ for 0≤θ≤π?

a
2∫0πsin⁡θdθ
b
4∫0πcos2⁡θdθ
c
2∫0πsin2⁡θdθ
d
8∫0πcos⁡θdθ
e
8∫0πsin2⁡θdθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=2sin⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=2sin⁡θcos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=2sin2⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=2sin⁡θcos⁡θ and y=2sin2⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π.

Now, if f(x,y)=x2+y2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=(2sin⁡θcos⁡θ)2+(2sin2⁡θ)2=4sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+4sin4⁡θ=4sin2⁡θ(cos2⁡θ+sin2⁡θ)=4sin2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2sin⁡θ)=2cos⁡θ,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(2sin⁡θ)2+(2cos⁡θ)2=4sin2⁡θ+4cos2⁡θ=4(sin2⁡θ+cos2⁡θ)=2.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫C(x2+y2)ds=∫0πf(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π4sin2⁡θ⋅2⋅dθ=8∫0πsin2⁡θdθ.

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\sqrt{2}$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}?$
question.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{2})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{2})^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cx2yds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=2 for −π4≤θ≤π4?

a
4∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ
b
4∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos⁡θdθ
c
22∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos⁡θdθ
d
2∫−π/4π/4sin2⁡θcos⁡θdθ
e
2∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=2cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=2cos⁡θ and y=2sin⁡θ, where −π4≤θ≤π4.

Now, if f(x,y)=x2y, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=(2cos⁡θ)2⋅2sin⁡θ=22sin⁡θcos2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(2)2+02=2.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cx2yds=∫−π/4π/4f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/4π/422sin⁡θcos2⁡θ⋅2⋅dθ=4∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ.

last_observation.name: Question 2
last_observation.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{2})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{2})^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cx2yds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=2 for −π4≤θ≤π4?

a
4∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ
b
4∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos⁡θdθ
c
22∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos⁡θdθ
d
2∫−π/4π/4sin2⁡θcos⁡θdθ
e
2∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=2cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=2cos⁡θ and y=2sin⁡θ, where −π4≤θ≤π4.

Now, if f(x,y)=x2y, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=(2cos⁡θ)2⋅2sin⁡θ=22sin⁡θcos2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(2)2+02=2.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cx2yds=∫−π/4π/4f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/4π/422sin⁡θcos2⁡θ⋅2⋅dθ=4∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ.

solution.reasoning: Using x=√2 cosθ, y=√2 sinθ, and ds=√2 dθ gives x²y ds=4sinθ cos²θ dθ, so option a is the direct polar-coordinate conversion. The integral is zero by oddness; options b, c, and e also evaluate to zero, making literal numerical equivalence nonunique. No Math Academy answer evidence was supplied.

feedback.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\sqrt{2}$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\sqrt{2})=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(\sqrt{2})^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \sqrt{2}\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =4{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cx2yds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=2 for −π4≤θ≤π4?

a
4∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ
b
4∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos⁡θdθ
c
22∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos⁡θdθ
d
2∫−π/4π/4sin2⁡θcos⁡θdθ
e
2∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=2cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=2cos⁡θ and y=2sin⁡θ, where −π4≤θ≤π4.

Now, if f(x,y)=x2y, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=(2cos⁡θ)2⋅2sin⁡θ=22sin⁡θcos2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(2)2+02=2.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cx2yds=∫−π/4π/4f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/4π/422sin⁡θcos2⁡θ⋅2⋅dθ=4∫−π/4π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ.

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=2$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}?$
question.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(2)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cxy2ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=2 for 0≤θ≤π4?

a
32∫0π/4(sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ)2dθ
b
8∫0π/4sin2⁡θcos4⁡θdθ
c
8∫0π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ
d
4∫0π/4(sin⁡θ+cos2⁡θ)dθ
e
16∫0π/4cos⁡θsin2⁡θdθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=2cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=2cos⁡θ and y=2sin⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π4.

Now, if f(x,y)=xy2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=2cos⁡θ⋅(2sin⁡θ)2=8cos⁡θsin2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(2)2+02=2.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cxy2ds=∫0π/4f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/48cos⁡θsin2⁡θ⋅2⋅dθ=16∫0π/4cos⁡θsin2⁡θdθ.

last_observation.name: Question 3
last_observation.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(2)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cxy2ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=2 for 0≤θ≤π4?

a
32∫0π/4(sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ)2dθ
b
8∫0π/4sin2⁡θcos4⁡θdθ
c
8∫0π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ
d
4∫0π/4(sin⁡θ+cos2⁡θ)dθ
e
16∫0π/4cos⁡θsin2⁡θdθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=2cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=2cos⁡θ and y=2sin⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π4.

Now, if f(x,y)=xy2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=2cos⁡θ⋅(2sin⁡θ)2=8cos⁡θsin2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(2)2+02=2.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cxy2ds=∫0π/4f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/48cos⁡θsin2⁡θ⋅2⋅dθ=16∫0π/4cos⁡θsin2⁡θdθ.

solution.reasoning: With x=2cosθ, y=2sinθ, and ds=2dθ, we obtain xy² ds=16cosθ sin²θ dθ. Thus option e is the equivalent integral. No captured Math Academy answer or grading evidence establishes its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 3
feedback.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=2$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta =2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{4}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x{y}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot (2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2} \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(2)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{(2)^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

 

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}8\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot 2\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{\pi /4}\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cxy2ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=2 for 0≤θ≤π4?

a
32∫0π/4(sin⁡θ+cos⁡θ)2dθ
b
8∫0π/4sin2⁡θcos4⁡θdθ
c
8∫0π/4sin⁡θcos2⁡θdθ
d
4∫0π/4(sin⁡θ+cos2⁡θ)dθ
e
16∫0π/4cos⁡θsin2⁡θdθ
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=2cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=2sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=2cos⁡θ and y=2sin⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π4.

Now, if f(x,y)=xy2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=2cos⁡θ⋅(2sin⁡θ)2=8cos⁡θsin2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(2)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(2)2+02=2.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cxy2ds=∫0π/4f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/48cos⁡θsin2⁡θ⋅2⋅dθ=16∫0π/4cos⁡θsin2⁡θdθ.

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}x(1-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=1\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{8}?$
question.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{8}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x(1-{y}^{2})$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+0} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x(1-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cx(1−y2)ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=1 for 0≤θ≤π8?

a
∫0π/8cos2⁡θsin2⁡θdθ
b
2∫0π/8sin2⁡θdθ
c
∫0π/8cos3⁡θdθ
d
2∫0π/8cos2⁡θdθ
e
4∫0π/8cos2⁡θsin⁡θdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=1⋅cos⁡θ=cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=1⋅sin⁡θ=sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=cos⁡θ and y=sin⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π8.

Now, if f(x,y)=x(1−y2), we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=cos⁡θ(1−sin2⁡θ)=cos⁡θ⋅cos2⁡θ=cos3⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(1)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=12+02=1+0=1.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cx(1−y2)ds=∫0π/8f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/8cos3⁡θ⋅1⋅dθ=∫0π/8cos3⁡θdθ.

last_observation.name: Question 4
last_observation.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{8}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x(1-{y}^{2})$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+0} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x(1-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cx(1−y2)ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=1 for 0≤θ≤π8?

a
∫0π/8cos2⁡θsin2⁡θdθ
b
2∫0π/8sin2⁡θdθ
c
∫0π/8cos3⁡θdθ
d
2∫0π/8cos2⁡θdθ
e
4∫0π/8cos2⁡θsin⁡θdθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rcos⁡θ=1⋅cos⁡θ=cos⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=1⋅sin⁡θ=sin⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=cos⁡θ and y=sin⁡θ, where 0≤θ≤π8.

Now, if f(x,y)=x(1−y2), we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=cos⁡θ(1−sin2⁡θ)=cos⁡θ⋅cos2⁡θ=cos3⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(1)=0,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=12+02=1+0=1.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cx(1−y2)ds=∫0π/8f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫0π/8cos3⁡θ⋅1⋅dθ=∫0π/8cos3⁡θdθ.

solution.reasoning: For r=1, x=cosθ, y=sinθ, and ds=dθ. Therefore x(1−y²)ds=cosθ(1−sin²θ)dθ=cos³θ dθ, giving option c. No captured Math Academy answer or grading evidence establishes its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 4
feedback.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}x(1-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=1\,$ for $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{8}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta , \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =1\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta $, where $0\le \theta \le \frac{\pi }{8}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=x(1-{y}^{2})$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta (1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ) \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cdot {cos}^{2}⁡\theta  \\  & ={cos}^{3}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(1)=0,\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{1+0} \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x(1-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \cdot 1\cdot \text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /8}{cos}^{3}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le -\frac{\pi }{8}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }{{(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )=-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta },\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }+\frac{1}{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cy4x2ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=cot⁡θ for −π4≤θ≤−π8?

a
∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
b
∫−π/4−π/8cos2⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
c
∫−π/4−π/8sin⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
d
∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
e
∫−π/4−π/8cos⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rsin⁡θ=cot⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=cos⁡θsin⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=cos2⁡θsin⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=cot⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=cos⁡θsin⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=cos⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=cos2⁡θsin⁡θ and y=cos⁡θ, where −π4≤θ≤−π8.

Now, if f(x,y)=y4x2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=cos4⁡θ(cos2⁡θsin⁡θ)2=sin2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(cot⁡θ)=−1sin2⁡θ,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(cot⁡θ)2+(−1sin2⁡θ)2=cos2⁡θsin2⁡θ+1sin4⁡θ=sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1sin4⁡θ=sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1sin2⁡θ.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cy4x2ds=∫−π/4−π/8f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θ⋅sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1sin2⁡θdθ=∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ.

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le -\frac{\pi }{8}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }{{(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )=-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta },\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }+\frac{1}{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

question.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cy4x2ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=cot⁡θ for −π4≤θ≤−π8?

a
∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
b
∫−π/4−π/8cos2⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
c
∫−π/4−π/8sin⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
d
∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
e
∫−π/4−π/8cos⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rsin⁡θ=cot⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=cos⁡θsin⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=cos2⁡θsin⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=cot⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=cos⁡θsin⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=cos⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=cos2⁡θsin⁡θ and y=cos⁡θ, where −π4≤θ≤−π8.

Now, if f(x,y)=y4x2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=cos4⁡θ(cos2⁡θsin⁡θ)2=sin2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(cot⁡θ)=−1sin2⁡θ,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(cot⁡θ)2+(−1sin2⁡θ)2=cos2⁡θsin2⁡θ+1sin4⁡θ=sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1sin4⁡θ=sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1sin2⁡θ.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cy4x2ds=∫−π/4−π/8f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θ⋅sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1sin2⁡θdθ=∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ.

solution.reasoning: Substituting x=r cosθ and y=r sinθ gives y⁴/x²=r²sin⁴θ/cos²θ=sin²θ. Since r=cotθ and r′=−csc²θ, ds=√(cot²θ+csc⁴θ)dθ=√(sin²θ cos²θ+1)/sin²θ dθ. Multiplication cancels sin²θ, yielding option d. No captured Math Academy answer or grading evidence establishes its stated key.

feedback.name: Question 5
feedback.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the section of the polar curve $r=\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \,$ for $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le -\frac{\pi }{8}?$
feedback.worked_solution:
In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

 

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }, \\ y & =r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta \cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡\theta  \\  & =\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

So, along our curve, we have $x=\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }$ and $y=\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, where $-\frac{\pi }{4}\le \theta \le -\frac{\pi }{8}.$

Now, if $f(x,y)=\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ) & =\frac{{cos}^{4}⁡\theta }{{(\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & ={sin}^{2}⁡\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta } & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}\theta }(\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )=-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta },\end{aligned}
$$

and therefore

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  & =\sqrt{{(\operatorname{cot}⁡\theta )}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta })}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }+\frac{1}{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\sqrt{\frac{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}{{sin}^{4}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{{y}^{4}}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}}{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta }\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /4}^{-\pi /8}\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta +1}\,\text{d}\theta .\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to the integral ∫Cy4x2ds, where C is the section of the polar curve r=cot⁡θ for −π4≤θ≤−π8?

a
∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
b
∫−π/4−π/8cos2⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
c
∫−π/4−π/8sin⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
d
∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
e
∫−π/4−π/8cos⁡θsin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

In polar coordinates, the formula for the line integral is given by

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫θ1θ2f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

The connection between polar and Cartesian coordinates gives

x=rsin⁡θ=cot⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=cos⁡θsin⁡θ⋅cos⁡θ=cos2⁡θsin⁡θ,y=rsin⁡θ=cot⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=cos⁡θsin⁡θ⋅sin⁡θ=cos⁡θ.

So, along our curve, we have x=cos2⁡θsin⁡θ and y=cos⁡θ, where −π4≤θ≤−π8.

Now, if f(x,y)=y4x2, we obtain

f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)=cos4⁡θ(cos2⁡θsin⁡θ)2=sin2⁡θ.

Next, we have

drdθ=ddθ(cot⁡θ)=−1sin2⁡θ,

and therefore

r2+(drdθ)2dθ=(cot⁡θ)2+(−1sin2⁡θ)2=cos2⁡θsin2⁡θ+1sin4⁡θ=sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1sin4⁡θ=sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1sin2⁡θ.

Finally, we can write the integral as

∫Cy4x2ds=∫−π/4−π/8f(rcos⁡θ,rsin⁡θ)r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θ⋅sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1sin2⁡θdθ=∫−π/4−π/8sin2⁡θcos2⁡θ+1dθ.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
For $x,y,z\in {R}^{2},$ consider the following functions: 

$$
\begin{aligned} & y(x)=Ax\,\text{where}\,A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & z(y)=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{2} \\ {y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & f(z)=Cz\,\text{where}\,C=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))$ evaluated at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $z\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $C$ and outputs a vector $f(z)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}=C.
$$

- The function $z$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $z(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2{y}_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & 2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=A{x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}2(1) & 0 \\ 0 & 2(3)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $A$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=A.
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x))){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}{|}_{{z}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 44 \\ 18 & 24\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the functions $y:{R}^{3}\to {R}^{2}$ and $f:{R}^{2}\to {R}^{2},$ defined by $$ y(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3} \\ {x}_{1}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3}\end{aligned}],\,f(y)=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}-{y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}]. $$ What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))$ evaluated at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]?$
${\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))|}_{{x}_{0}}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} {{field-3}}
$38$ {{field-4}} $34$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2{y}_{1} & 2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=[\begin{aligned}3\cdot 2+1 \\ 3+2\cdot 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 5\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 14 & 10\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{3}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & {x}_{1} & 1 \\ 1 & {x}_{3} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 14 & 10\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & -1 \\ 38 & 52 & 34\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the functions $y(x)=Ax$ and $f(y)=By,$ where $x\in {R}^{2},y\in {R}^{3},$ and the matrices $A$ and $B$ are given by $$ A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 4 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 2 & -1\end{aligned}],\,B=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 & -1 \\ 4 & 1 & 2\end{aligned}]. $$ What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))$ evaluated at ${x}_{0}=[0,\,1]^{T}?$
${\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))|}_{{x}_{0}}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}}
$11$ {{field-3}}

Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{3}$ by multiplying it by $B$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}=B.
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $A$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{3}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=A.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$

$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
For $x,y,z\in {R}^{2},$ consider the following functions: 

$$
\begin{aligned} & y(x)=Ax\,\text{where}\,A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & z(y)=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}{y}_{2} \\ {y}_{1}+{y}_{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & f(z)=Cz\,\text{where}\,C=[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))$ evaluated at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]?$
questions.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $z\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $C$ and outputs a vector $f(z)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}=C.
$$

- The function $z$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $z(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{2} & {y}_{1} \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=A{x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $A$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=A.
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x))){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}{|}_{{z}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 2 \\ 1 & 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & -2 \\ 5 & 4\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ 13 & -5\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{3}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{2}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}(2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}^{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}(2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}^{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2{y}_{2} \\ 2 & 3{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=[\begin{aligned}0-{1}^{3} \\ -1\cdot 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}-{x}_{1}^{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}-{x}_{1}^{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(-{x}_{1}{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(-{x}_{1}{x}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{1}^{2} & 1 \\ -{x}_{2} & -{x}_{1}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \\ -6 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}^{2}+{y}_{2}^{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 2{y}_{1} & 2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=[\begin{aligned}3\cdot 2+1 \\ 3+2\cdot 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 5\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 14 & 10\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{3}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 3$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{3}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{3}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{3}}({x}_{1}+{x}_{2}{x}_{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}{x}_{2} & {x}_{1} & 1 \\ 1 & {x}_{3} & {x}_{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$

Question 4
?

For x,y,z∈R2, consider the following functions:

y(x)=AxwhereA=[1−120]z(y)=[y1y2y1+y2]f(z)=CzwhereC=[4215] What is ddxf(z(y(x))) evaluated at x0=[01]?

a
[−5312]
b
[13−24]
c
[4−20−5]
d
[−2−213−5]
e
[2−2−135]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Using the chain rule, we have

ddxf(z(y(x)))=dfdz⋅dzdy⋅dydx.

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

  • The function f acts on a vector z∈R2 by multiplying it by C and outputs a vector f(z)∈R2. Thus, dfdz=C.

  • The function z acts on a vector y∈R2 and outputs a vector z(y)∈R2. Thus, dzdy=[∂z1∂y1∂z1∂y2∂z2∂y1∂z2∂y2]=[y2y111]. Evaluating at y0=Ax0=[1−120][01]=[−10], we get dzdy|y0=[0−111].

  • The function y acts on a vector x∈R2 by multiplying it by A and outputs a vector y(x)∈R2. Thus, dydx=A.

Therefore, we have

ddxf(z(y(x)))|x0=dfdz|z0⋅dzdy|y0⋅dydx|x0=[4215]⋅[0−111]⋅[1−120]=[2−254]⋅[1−120]=[−2−213−5].

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $f(y)\in {R}^{3}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $f$ with respect to $y$ is a $3\times 2$ matrix 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{f}_{3}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{1}-{y}_{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}({y}_{2}^{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}({y}_{2}^{2}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{1}}(2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}^{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{y}_{2}}(2{y}_{1}+{y}_{2}^{3})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 2{y}_{2} \\ 2 & 3{y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=y({x}_{0})=[\begin{aligned}0-{1}^{3} \\ -1\cdot 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus, the total derivative of $y$ with respect to $x$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{1}}{∂{x}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{1}} & \frac{∂{y}_{2}}{∂{x}_{2}}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}({x}_{2}-{x}_{1}^{3}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}({x}_{2}-{x}_{1}^{3}) \\ \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{1}}(-{x}_{1}{x}_{2}) & \frac{∂}{∂{x}_{2}}(-{x}_{1}{x}_{2})\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3{x}_{1}^{2} & 1 \\ -{x}_{2} & -{x}_{1}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \\ -6 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluating at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}].

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(y(x)){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 0 & -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 2 \\ 0 & 0 \\ -6 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 1
question.problem:
For $x,y,z\in {R}^{2},$ consider the following functions: 

$$
\begin{aligned} & y(x)=Ax\,\text{where}\,A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & z(y)=[\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}^{2} \\ {y}_{2}^{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & f(z)=Cz\,\text{where}\,C=[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

What is $\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))$ evaluated at ${x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]?$
question.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $z\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $C$ and outputs a vector $f(z)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}=C.
$$

- The function $z$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $z(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2{y}_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & 2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=A{x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}2(1) & 0 \\ 0 & 2(3)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $A$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=A.
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x))){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}{|}_{{z}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 44 \\ 18 & 24\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

For x,y,z∈R2, consider the following functions:

y(x)=AxwhereA=[1234]z(y)=[y12y22]f(z)=CzwhereC=[5101] What is ddxf(z(y(x))) evaluated at x0=[10]?

a
[28441824]
b
[28184424]
c
[1824]
d
[1824]
e
 [8184424]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Using the chain rule, we have

ddxf(z(y(x)))=dfdz⋅dzdy⋅dydx.

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

  • The function f acts on a vector z∈R2 by multiplying it by C and outputs a vector f(z)∈R2. Thus, dfdz=C.

  • The function z acts on a vector y∈R2 and outputs a vector z(y)∈R2. Thus, dzdy=[∂z1∂y1∂z1∂y2∂z2∂y1∂z2∂y2]=[2y1002y2]. Evaluating at y0=Ax0=[1234][10]=[13], we get dzdy|y0=[2(1)002(3)]=[2006].

  • The function y acts on a vector x∈R2 by multiplying it by A and outputs a vector y(x)∈R2. Thus, dydx=A.

Therefore, we have

ddxf(z(y(x)))|x0=dfdz|z0⋅dzdy|y0⋅dydx|x0=[5101]⋅[2006]⋅[1234]=[10606]⋅[1234]=[28441824].

last_observation.worked_solution:
Using the chain rule, we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x)))=\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}.
$$

Let's consider each of the factors in turn.

- The function $f$ acts on a vector $z\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $C$ and outputs a vector $f(z)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}=C.
$$

- The function $z$ acts on a vector $y\in {R}^{2}$ and outputs a vector $z(y)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{1}}{∂{y}_{2}} \\ \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{1}} & \frac{∂{z}_{2}}{∂{y}_{2}}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2{y}_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & 2{y}_{2}\end{aligned}].
$$

Evaluating at ${y}_{0}=A{x}_{0}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 3\end{aligned}],$ we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}=[\begin{aligned}2(1) & 0 \\ 0 & 2(3)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

- The function $y$ acts on a vector $x\in {R}^{2}$ by multiplying it by $A$ and outputs a vector $y(x)\in {R}^{2}.$ Thus,

$$
\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=A.
$$

Therefore, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}f(z(y(x))){|}_{{x}_{0}} & =\frac{\text{d}f}{\text{d}z}{|}_{{z}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}y}{|}_{{y}_{0}}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}{|}_{{x}_{0}} \\  & =[\begin{aligned}5 & 1 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 0 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}10 & 6 \\ 0 & 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}28 & 44 \\ 18 & 24\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
