$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Since our surface $S$ is of the form $z=g(x,y),$ it can be parameterized as

$$
r(x,y)=⟨x,\,y,\,g(x,y)⟩.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′} & =⟨1,\,0,\,\frac{∂g}{∂x}⟩ \\ {r}_{y}^{′} & =⟨0,\,1,\,\frac{∂g}{∂y}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′} & =|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & \frac{∂g}{∂x} \\ 0 & 1 & \frac{∂g}{∂y}\end{aligned}|=⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(x,y))\cdot ({r}_{x}^{′}\times {r}_{y}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩\cdot ⟨-\frac{∂g}{∂x},\,-\frac{∂g}{∂y},\,1⟩\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

For a surface S given by z=g(x,y) for (x,y)∈D, the flux of the vector field F(x,y,z)=⟨P,Q,R⟩ over S is given by ∬SF⋅dS=∬D(−P∂gA−QA∂y+A)dA. From left to right, what are the missing parts of the formula?

a
∂x,∂g, and −R
b
∂x,∂g, and R
c
∂z,∂g, and −1
d
∂x,∂g, and −1
e
 ∂x,∂g, and 1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a surface S with parametrization r(u,v) for (u,v)∈D, the flux of a vector field F over S is given by

∬SF⋅dS=∬SF⋅ndS=∬DF(r(u,v))⋅(ru′×rv′)dA.

Since our surface S is of the form z=g(x,y), it can be parameterized as

r(x,y)=⟨x,y,g(x,y)⟩.

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

rx′=⟨1,0,∂g∂x⟩ry′=⟨0,1,∂g∂y⟩

Now, the fundamental vector product is

rx′×ry′=|ijk10∂g∂x01∂g∂y|=⟨−∂g∂x,−∂g∂y,1⟩.

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

∬SF⋅dS=∬DF(r(x,y))⋅(rx′×ry′)dA=∬D⟨P,Q,R⟩⋅⟨−∂g∂x,−∂g∂y,1⟩dA=∬D(−P∂g∂x−Q∂g∂y+R)dA.

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}$ at the point $(1,1,1,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=-4z\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1) & =2\cdot 1=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1) & =2\cdot 1=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) & =-4\cdot 1=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) \\ w & =2(x-1)+2(y-1)-4(z-1) \\ w & =2x-2+2y-2-4z+4 \\ -2x-2y+4z+w & =0 \\ 2x+2y-4z-w & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem: At which points on the surface $z=x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v\,=\,⟨-2,4,2⟩?$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}) \\  & ={e}^{y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}) \\  & =x{e}^{y}+2y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨{e}^{y},\,x{e}^{y}+2y,\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨-2,4,2⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨{e}^{y},\,x{e}^{y}+2y,\,-1⟩=⟨-2,4,2⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}c{e}^{y}=-2 \\ cx{e}^{y}+2cy=4 \\ -c=2\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-2{e}^{y}=-2\,⟹\,y=0.
$$

And substituting $c=-2$ and $y=0$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
-2x{e}^{0}+2(-2)(0)=4\,⟹\,x=-2.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-2$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2} \\  & =(-2){e}^{0}+{0}^{2} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(-2,0,-2).$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z}$ at the point $(1,9,4,2).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,9,4):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,9,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1}}=\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,9,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{9}}=\frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,9,4) & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}}=-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-2 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,9,4)+(y-9)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,9,4)+(z-4)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,9,4) \\ w-2 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1)+\frac{1}{6}(y-9)-\frac{1}{4}(z-4) \\ w-2 & =\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{6}y-\frac{1}{4}z-1 \\ \frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{6}y-\frac{1}{4}z-w+1 & =0 \\ 12(\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{6}y-\frac{1}{4}z-w+1) & =12\cdot 0 \\ 6x+2y-3z-12w+12 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem: At which points on the surface $z=8{x}^{3}-12xy+{y}^{3}+1$ is the tangent plane horizontal?
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{x}^{3}-12xy+{y}^{3}+1) \\  & =24{x}^{2}-12y \\  & =12(2{x}^{2}-y) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(8{x}^{3}-12xy+{y}^{3}+1) \\  & =-12x+3{y}^{2} \\  & =3({y}^{2}-4x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨12(2{x}^{2}-y),\,3({y}^{2}-4x),\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}12(2{x}^{2}-y)=0 \\ 3({y}^{2}-4x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $y=2{x}^{2}.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3({(2{x}^{2})}^{2}-4x) & =0 \\ 4{x}^{4}-4x & =0 \\ 4x({x}^{3}-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions of the last equation are $x=0,1.$ So, we have two cases.

- For $x=0,$ we have 

$$
y=2({0}^{2})=0.
$$

Now, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z=8({0}^{3})-12(0)(0)+{0}^{3}+1=1.
$$

So, our first point is $(0,0,1).$

- For $x=1,$ we have 

$$
y=2({1}^{2})=2.
$$

Now, substituting $x=1$ and $y=2$ into our function, we get

$$
z=8({1}^{3})-12(1)(2)+{2}^{3}+1=-7.
$$

So, our second point is $(1,2,-7).$

Therefore, the points where the tangent plane is horizontal are $(0,0,1)$ and $(1,2,-7).$

\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2})=-4x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2})=-10y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨-2,-5,1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩=⟨-2,-5,1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4cx=-2 \\ -10cy=-5 \\ -c=1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-4(-1)x=-2\,⟹\,x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

And substituting $c=-1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
-10(-1)y=-5\,⟹\,y=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $y=-\frac{1}{2}$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =4-2{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-5{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =4-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{5}{4} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2},\frac{9}{4}).$

observed_steps.name: Question 1
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=-4z\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1) & =2\cdot 1=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1) & =2\cdot 1=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) & =-4\cdot 1=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) \\ w & =2(x-1)+2(y-1)-4(z-1) \\ w & =2x-2+2y-2-4z+4 \\ -2x-2y+4z+w & =0 \\ 2x+2y-4z-w & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface w=x2+y2−2z2 at the point (1,1,1,0).

a
2x−2y−4z+w+4=0
b
2x−2y+4z−w−4=0
c
2x+2y−4z+w=0
d
2x+2y+4z−w−8=0
e
2x+2y−4z−w=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface w=f(x,y,z) at the point (x0,y0,z0,w0) on the hypersurface can be written as

w−w0=(x−x0)∂f∂x(x0,y0,z0)+(y−y0)∂f∂y(x0,y0,z0)+(z−z0)∂f∂z(x0,y0,z0).

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂f∂x=∂∂x(x2+y2−2z2)=2x∂f∂y=∂∂y(x2+y2−2z2)=2y∂f∂z=∂∂z(x2+y2−2z2)=−4z

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at (x,y,z)=(1,1,1):

∂f∂x(1,1,1)=2⋅1=2∂f∂y(1,1,1)=2⋅1=2∂f∂z(1,1,1)=−4⋅1=−4

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

w−0=(x−1)∂f∂x(1,1,1)+(y−1)∂f∂y(1,1,1)+(z−1)∂f∂z(1,1,1)w=2(x−1)+2(y−1)−4(z−1)w=2x−2+2y−2−4z+4−2x−2y+4z+w=02x+2y−4z−w=0

observed_steps.name: Question 2
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}) \\  & ={e}^{y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}) \\  & =x{e}^{y}+2y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨{e}^{y},\,x{e}^{y}+2y,\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨-2,4,2⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨{e}^{y},\,x{e}^{y}+2y,\,-1⟩=⟨-2,4,2⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}c{e}^{y}=-2 \\ cx{e}^{y}+2cy=4 \\ -c=2\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-2{e}^{y}=-2\,⟹\,y=0.
$$

And substituting $c=-2$ and $y=0$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
-2x{e}^{0}+2(-2)(0)=4\,⟹\,x=-2.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-2$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2} \\  & =(-2){e}^{0}+{0}^{2} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(-2,0,-2).$

observed_steps.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{x}^{3}-12xy+{y}^{3}+1) \\  & =24{x}^{2}-12y \\  & =12(2{x}^{2}-y) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(8{x}^{3}-12xy+{y}^{3}+1) \\  & =-12x+3{y}^{2} \\  & =3({y}^{2}-4x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨12(2{x}^{2}-y),\,3({y}^{2}-4x),\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}12(2{x}^{2}-y)=0 \\ 3({y}^{2}-4x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $y=2{x}^{2}.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3({(2{x}^{2})}^{2}-4x) & =0 \\ 4{x}^{4}-4x & =0 \\ 4x({x}^{3}-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions of the last equation are $x=0,1.$ So, we have two cases.

- For $x=0,$ we have 

$$
y=2({0}^{2})=0.
$$

Now, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z=8({0}^{3})-12(0)(0)+{0}^{3}+1=1.
$$

So, our first point is $(0,0,1).$

- For $x=1,$ we have 

$$
y=2({1}^{2})=2.
$$

Now, substituting $x=1$ and $y=2$ into our function, we get

$$
z=8({1}^{3})-12(1)(2)+{2}^{3}+1=-7.
$$

So, our second point is $(1,2,-7).$

Therefore, the points where the tangent plane is horizontal are $(0,0,1)$ and $(1,2,-7).$

Question 4
?

At which points on the surface z=8x3−12xy+y3+1 is the tangent plane horizontal?

a
(0,2,9) and (1,1,−2)
b
(0,0,1) only
c
(0,2,9) only
d
(1,1,−2) only
e
(0,0,1) and (1,2,−7)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface z=f(x,y) at the point (x0,y0,z0) on the surface can be written as z−z0=(x−x0)∂f∂x(x0,y0)+(y−y0)∂f∂y(x0,y0), where ⟨∂f∂x(x0,y0),∂f∂y(x0,y0),−1⟩ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives: ∂f∂x=∂∂x(8x3−12xy+y3+1)=24x2−12y=12(2x2−y)∂f∂y=∂∂y(8x3−12xy+y3+1)=−12x+3y2=3(y2−4x)

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is ⟨12(2x2−y),3(y2−4x),−1⟩.

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the x- and y-components of the vector must be 0: {∂f∂x=0∂f∂y=0⟹{12(2x2−y)=03(y2−4x)=0

From the first equation, we get y=2x2. Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 3((2x2)2−4x)=04x4−4x=04x(x3−1)=0. The solutions of the last equation are x=0,1. So, we have two cases.

  • For x=0, we have y=2(02)=0. Now, substituting x=0 and y=0 into our function, we get z=8(03)−12(0)(0)+03+1=1. So, our first point is (0,0,1).

  • For x=1, we have y=2(12)=2. Now, substituting x=1 and y=2 into our function, we get z=8(13)−12(1)(2)+23+1=−7. So, our second point is (1,2,−7).

Therefore, the points where the tangent plane is horizontal are (0,0,1) and (1,2,−7).

observed_steps.name: Question 5
observed_steps.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2})=-4x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2})=-10y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨-2,-5,1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩=⟨-2,-5,1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4cx=-2 \\ -10cy=-5 \\ -c=1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-4(-1)x=-2\,⟹\,x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

And substituting $c=-1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
-10(-1)y=-5\,⟹\,y=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $y=-\frac{1}{2}$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =4-2{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-5{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =4-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{5}{4} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2},\frac{9}{4}).$

Question 5
?

At which point on the surface z=4−2x2−5y2 is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector v=⟨−2,−5,1⟩?

a
(12,1,−32)
b
(−1,1,−3)
c
(−12,−12,94)
d
(2,−1,−9)
e
(1,0,2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface z=f(x,y) at the point (x0,y0,z0) on the surface can be written as z−z0=(x−x0)∂f∂x(x0,y0)+(y−y0)∂f∂y(x0,y0), where ⟨∂f∂x(x0,y0),∂f∂y(x0,y0),−1⟩ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives: ∂f∂x=∂∂x(4−2x2−5y2)=−4x∂f∂y=∂∂y(4−2x2−5y2)=−10y

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is ⟨−4x,−10y,−1⟩.

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to ⟨−2,−5,1⟩. So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant c, we must have c⋅⟨−4x,−10y,−1⟩=⟨−2,−5,1⟩.

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system: {−4cx=−2−10cy=−5−c=1

From the third equation, we get c=−1. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain −4(−1)x=−2⟹x=−12.

And substituting c=−1 into the second equation, we have −10(−1)y=−5⟹y=−12.

Finally, substituting x=−12 and y=−12 into our function, we get z=4−2(−12)2−5(−12)2=4−12−54=94.

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector v at (−12,−12,94).

question.name: Question 1
question.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}$ at the point $(1,1,1,0).$
question.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=-4z\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1) & =2\cdot 1=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1) & =2\cdot 1=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) & =-4\cdot 1=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) \\ w & =2(x-1)+2(y-1)-4(z-1) \\ w & =2x-2+2y-2-4z+4 \\ -2x-2y+4z+w & =0 \\ 2x+2y-4z-w & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1

Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface w=x2+y2−2z2 at the point (1,1,1,0).

a
2x−2y−4z+w+4=0
b
2x−2y+4z−w−4=0
c
2x+2y−4z+w=0
d
2x+2y+4z−w−8=0
e
2x+2y−4z−w=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface w=f(x,y,z) at the point (x0,y0,z0,w0) on the hypersurface can be written as

w−w0=(x−x0)∂f∂x(x0,y0,z0)+(y−y0)∂f∂y(x0,y0,z0)+(z−z0)∂f∂z(x0,y0,z0).

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂f∂x=∂∂x(x2+y2−2z2)=2x∂f∂y=∂∂y(x2+y2−2z2)=2y∂f∂z=∂∂z(x2+y2−2z2)=−4z

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at (x,y,z)=(1,1,1):

∂f∂x(1,1,1)=2⋅1=2∂f∂y(1,1,1)=2⋅1=2∂f∂z(1,1,1)=−4⋅1=−4

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

last_observation.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=-4z\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1) & =2\cdot 1=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1) & =2\cdot 1=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) & =-4\cdot 1=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) \\ w & =2(x-1)+2(y-1)-4(z-1) \\ w & =2x-2+2y-2-4z+4 \\ -2x-2y+4z+w & =0 \\ 2x+2y-4z-w & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 1
?

Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface w=x2+y2−2z2 at the point (1,1,1,0).

a
2x−2y−4z+w+4=0
b
2x−2y+4z−w−4=0
c
2x+2y−4z+w=0
d
2x+2y+4z−w−8=0
e
2x+2y−4z−w=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface w=f(x,y,z) at the point (x0,y0,z0,w0) on the hypersurface can be written as

w−w0=(x−x0)∂f∂x(x0,y0,z0)+(y−y0)∂f∂y(x0,y0,z0)+(z−z0)∂f∂z(x0,y0,z0).

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂f∂x=∂∂x(x2+y2−2z2)=2x∂f∂y=∂∂y(x2+y2−2z2)=2y∂f∂z=∂∂z(x2+y2−2z2)=−4z

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at (x,y,z)=(1,1,1):

∂f∂x(1,1,1)=2⋅1=2∂f∂y(1,1,1)=2⋅1=2∂f∂z(1,1,1)=−4⋅1=−4

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

w−0=(x−1)∂f∂x(1,1,1)+(y−1)∂f∂y(1,1,1)+(z−1)∂f∂z(1,1,1)w=2(x−1)+2(y−1)−4(z−1)w=2x−2+2y−2−4z+4−2x−2y+4z+w=02x+2y−4z−w=0

solution.reasoning: For f(x,y,z)=x²+y²−2z², ∇f(1,1,1)=(2,2,−4). Thus the tangent hyperplane is w=2(x−1)+2(y−1)−4(z−1)=2x+2y−4z, giving option e. The mathematics is determined, but no Math Academy answer-key evidence was captured.

feedback.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w={x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2}$ at the point $(1,1,1,0).$
feedback.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-2{z}^{2})=-4z\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1) & =2\cdot 1=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1) & =2\cdot 1=2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) & =-4\cdot 1=-4\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,1)+(z-1)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,1) \\ w & =2(x-1)+2(y-1)-4(z-1) \\ w & =2x-2+2y-2-4z+4 \\ -2x-2y+4z+w & =0 \\ 2x+2y-4z-w & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 2
question.problem: At which points on the surface $z=x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v\,=\,⟨-2,4,2⟩?$
question.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}) \\  & ={e}^{y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}) \\  & =x{e}^{y}+2y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨{e}^{y},\,x{e}^{y}+2y,\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨-2,4,2⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨{e}^{y},\,x{e}^{y}+2y,\,-1⟩=⟨-2,4,2⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}c{e}^{y}=-2 \\ cx{e}^{y}+2cy=4 \\ -c=2\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-2{e}^{y}=-2\,⟹\,y=0.
$$

And substituting $c=-2$ and $y=0$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
-2x{e}^{0}+2(-2)(0)=4\,⟹\,x=-2.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-2$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$

∂f∂x=∂∂x(xey+y2)=ey∂f∂y=∂∂y(xey+y2)=xey+2y

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is

⟨ey,xey+2y,−1⟩

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

{cey=−2cxey+2cy=4−c=2

From the third equation, we get c=−2. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

−2ey=−2⟹y=0.

And substituting c=−2 and y=0 into the second equation, we have −2xe0+2(−2)(0)=4⟹x=−2.

Finally, substituting x=−2 and y=0 into our function, we get

z=xey+y2=(−2)e0+02=−2.

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector v at (−2,0,−2).

$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}) \\  & ={e}^{y} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2}) \\  & =x{e}^{y}+2y\end{aligned}
$$

$$
⟨{e}^{y},\,x{e}^{y}+2y,\,-1⟩
$$

$$
c\cdot ⟨{e}^{y},\,x{e}^{y}+2y,\,-1⟩=⟨-2,4,2⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}c{e}^{y}=-2 \\ cx{e}^{y}+2cy=4 \\ -c=2\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-2.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-2{e}^{y}=-2\,⟹\,y=0.
$$

And substituting $c=-2$ and $y=0$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
-2x{e}^{0}+2(-2)(0)=4\,⟹\,x=-2.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =x{e}^{y}+{y}^{2} \\  & =(-2){e}^{0}+{0}^{2} \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(-2,0,-2).$

z−z0=(x−x0)∂f∂x(x0,y0)+(y−y0)∂f∂y(x0,y0),

where ⟨∂f∂x(x0,y0),∂f∂y(x0,y0),−1⟩ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

∂f∂x=∂∂x(xey+y2)=ey∂f∂y=∂∂y(xey+y2)=xey+2y

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is

⟨ey,xey+2y,−1⟩

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to ⟨−2,4,2⟩. So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant c, we must have

c⋅⟨ey,xey+2y,−1⟩=⟨−2,4,2⟩.

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

{cey=−2cxey+2cy=4−c=2

From the third equation, we get c=−2. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain

−2ey=−2⟹y=0.

And substituting c=−2 and y=0 into the second equation, we have −2xe0+2(−2)(0)=4⟹x=−2.

Finally, substituting x=−2 and y=0 into our function, we get

z=xey+y2=(−2)e0+02=−2.

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector v at (−2,0,−2).

solution.reasoning: A normal to the tangent plane is (e^y,xe^y+2y,−1). For the plane to be perpendicular to v, this normal must be parallel to (−2,4,2). The third component gives proportionality factor −1/2, so e^y=1 and xe^y+2y=−2. Hence y=0, x=−2, and z=−2. Only option a is correct. No Math Academy answer-key evidence was provided.

⟨ey,xey+2y,−1⟩

{cey=−2cxey+2cy=4−c=2

question.name: Question 3
question.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z}$ at the point $(1,9,4,2).$
question.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,9,4):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,9,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1}}=\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,9,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{9}}=\frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,9,4) & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}}=-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-2 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,9,4)+(y-9)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,9,4)+(z-4)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,9,4) \\ w-2 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1)+\frac{1}{6}(y-9)-\frac{1}{4}(z-4) \\ w-2 & =\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{6}y-\frac{1}{4}z-1 \\ \frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{6}y-\frac{1}{4}z-w+1 & =0 \\ 12(\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{6}y-\frac{1}{4}z-w+1) & =12\cdot 0 \\ 6x+2y-3z-12w+12 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface w=x+y−z at the point (1,9,4,2).

2x−z−8w+18=0

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at (x,y,z)=(1,9,4): ∂f∂x(1,9,4)=121=12∂f∂y(1,9,4)=129=16∂f∂z(1,9,4)=−124=−14

last_observation.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,9,4):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,9,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1}}=\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,9,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{9}}=\frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,9,4) & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}}=-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-2 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,9,4)+(y-9)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,9,4)+(z-4)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,9,4) \\ w-2 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1)+\frac{1}{6}(y-9)-\frac{1}{4}(z-4) \\ w-2 & =\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{6}y-\frac{1}{4}z-1 \\ \frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{6}y-\frac{1}{4}z-w+1 & =0 \\ 12(\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{6}y-\frac{1}{4}z-w+1) & =12\cdot 0 \\ 6x+2y-3z-12w+12 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface w=x+y−z at the point (1,9,4,2).

a
x−y+z−4w+12=0
b
2x−z−8w+18=0
c
6x−y−2z+6w−1=0
d
6x+2y−3z−12w+12=0
e
3x−y−2z−4w+22=0
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface w=f(x,y,z) at the point (x0,y0,z0,w0) on the hypersurface can be written as w−w0=(x−x0)∂f∂x(x0,y0,z0)+(y−y0)∂f∂y(x0,y0,z0)+(z−z0)∂f∂z(x0,y0,z0).

First, we find the partial derivatives: ∂f∂x=∂∂x(x+y−z)=12x∂f∂y=∂∂y(x+y−z)=12y∂f∂z=∂∂z(x+y−z)=−12z

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at (x,y,z)=(1,9,4): ∂f∂x(1,9,4)=121=12∂f∂y(1,9,4)=129=16∂f∂z(1,9,4)=−124=−14

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane: w−2=(x−1)∂f∂x(1,9,4)+(y−9)∂f∂y(1,9,4)+(z−4)∂f∂z(1,9,4)w−2=12(x−1)+16(y−9)−14(z−4)w−2=12x+16y−14z−112x+16y−14z−w+1=012(12x+16y−14z−w+1)=12⋅06x+2y−3z−12w+12=0

solution.reasoning: The partial derivatives at (1,9,4) are 1/2, 1/6, and −1/4. Thus w−2=(x−1)/2+(y−9)/6−(z−4)/4. Multiplying by 12 and rearranging gives 6x+2y−3z−12w+12=0, option d. No Math Academy answer-key evidence was provided.

feedback.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z}$ at the point $(1,9,4,2).$
feedback.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})=\frac{1}{2\sqrt{y}} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(\sqrt{x}+\sqrt{y}-\sqrt{z})=-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{z}}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,9,4):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,9,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{1}}=\frac{1}{2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,9,4) & =\frac{1}{2\sqrt{9}}=\frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,9,4) & =-\frac{1}{2\sqrt{4}}=-\frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-2 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,9,4)+(y-9)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,9,4)+(z-4)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,9,4) \\ w-2 & =\frac{1}{2}(x-1)+\frac{1}{6}(y-9)-\frac{1}{4}(z-4) \\ w-2 & =\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{6}y-\frac{1}{4}z-1 \\ \frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{6}y-\frac{1}{4}z-w+1 & =0 \\ 12(\frac{1}{2}x+\frac{1}{6}y-\frac{1}{4}z-w+1) & =12\cdot 0 \\ 6x+2y-3z-12w+12 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

question.name: Question 4
question.problem: At which points on the surface $z=8{x}^{3}-12xy+{y}^{3}+1$ is the tangent plane horizontal?
question.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(8{x}^{3}-12xy+{y}^{3}+1) \\  & =24{x}^{2}-12y \\  & =12(2{x}^{2}-y) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(8{x}^{3}-12xy+{y}^{3}+1) \\  & =-12x+3{y}^{2} \\  & =3({y}^{2}-4x)\end{aligned}
$$

 

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨12(2{x}^{2}-y),\,3({y}^{2}-4x),\,-1⟩.
$$

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the $x$- and $y$-components of the vector must be $0:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}12(2{x}^{2}-y)=0 \\ 3({y}^{2}-4x)=0\end{aligned}
$$

 

From the first equation, we get $y=2{x}^{2}.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}3({(2{x}^{2})}^{2}-4x) & =0 \\ 4{x}^{4}-4x & =0 \\ 4x({x}^{3}-1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

The solutions of the last equation are $x=0,1.$ So, we have two cases.

- For $x=0,$ we have 

$$
y=2({0}^{2})=0.
$$

Now, substituting $x=0$ and $y=0$ into our function, we get

$$
z=8({0}^{3})-12(0)(0)+{0}^{3}+1=1.
$$

So, our first point is $(0,0,1).$

- For $x=1,$ we have 

$$
y=2({1}^{2})=2.
$$

Now, substituting $x=1$ and $y=2$ into our function, we get

$$
z=8({1}^{3})-12(1)(2)+{2}^{3}+1=-7.
$$

So, our second point is $(1,2,-7).$

Therefore, the points where the tangent plane is horizontal are $(0,0,1)$ and $(1,2,-7).$

Question 4
?

At which points on the surface z=8x3−12xy+y3+1 is the tangent plane horizontal?

a
(0,2,9) and (1,1,−2)
b
(0,0,1) only
c
(0,2,9) only
d
(1,1,−2) only
e
(0,0,1) and (1,2,−7)
Submit
Incorrect

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is ⟨12(2x2−y),3(y2−4x),−1⟩.

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the x- and y-components of the vector must be 0: {∂f∂x=0∂f∂y=0⟹{12(2x2−y)=03(y2−4x)=0

From the first equation, we get y=2x2. Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 3((2x2)2−4x)=04x4−4x=04x(x3−1)=0. The solutions of the last equation are x=0,1. So, we have two cases.

  • For x=0, we have y=2(02)=0. Now, substituting x=0 and y=0 into our function, we get z=8(03)−12(0)(0)+03+1=1. So, our first point is (0,0,1).

  • For x=1, we have y=2(12)=2. Now, substituting x=1 and y=2 into our function, we get z=8(13)−12(1)(2)+23+1=−7. So, our second point is (1,2,−7).

Therefore, the points where the tangent plane is horizontal are (0,0,1) and (1,2,−7).

$$

$$
⟨12(2{x}^{2}-y),\,3({y}^{2}-4x),\,-1⟩.
$$

\{\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}=0\end{aligned}\,⟹\,\{\begin{aligned}12(2{x}^{2}-y)=0 \\ 3({y}^{2}-4x)=0\end{aligned}

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the x- and y-components of the vector must be 0: {∂f∂x=0∂f∂y=0⟹{12(2x2−y)=03(y2−4x)=0

From the first equation, we get y=2x2. Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 3((2x2)2−4x)=04x4−4x=04x(x3−1)=0. The solutions of the last equation are x=0,1. So, we have two cases.

  • For x=0, we have y=2(02)=0. Now, substituting x=0 and y=0 into our function, we get z=8(03)−12(0)(0)+03+1=1. So, our first point is (0,0,1).

  • For x=1, we have y=2(12)=2. Now, substituting x=1 and y=2 into our function, we get z=8(13)−12(1)(2)+23+1=−7. So, our second point is (1,2,−7).

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is ⟨12(2x2−y),3(y2−4x),−1⟩.

Note that the tangent plane is horizontal if and only if the normal vector is vertical. This means that the x- and y-components of the vector must be 0: {∂f∂x=0∂f∂y=0⟹{12(2x2−y)=03(y2−4x)=0

From the first equation, we get y=2x2. Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 3((2x2)2−4x)=04x4−4x=04x(x3−1)=0. The solutions of the last equation are x=0,1. So, we have two cases.

  • For x=0, we have y=2(02)=0. Now, substituting x=0 and y=0 into our function, we get z=8(03)−12(0)(0)+03+1=1. So, our first point is (0,0,1).

  • For x=1, we have y=2(12)=2. Now, substituting x=1 and y=2 into our function, we get z=8(13)−12(1)(2)+23+1=−7. So, our second point is (1,2,−7).

question.name: Question 5
question.problem: At which point on the surface $z=4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector $v=⟨-2,-5,1⟩?$
question.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2})=-4x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2})=-10y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨-2,-5,1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩=⟨-2,-5,1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4cx=-2 \\ -10cy=-5 \\ -c=1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-4(-1)x=-2\,⟹\,x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

And substituting $c=-1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
-10(-1)y=-5\,⟹\,y=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $y=-\frac{1}{2}$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =4-2{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-5{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =4-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{5}{4} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2},\frac{9}{4}).$

last_observation.name: Question 5
last_observation.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2})=-4x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2})=-10y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨-2,-5,1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩=⟨-2,-5,1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4cx=-2 \\ -10cy=-5 \\ -c=1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-4(-1)x=-2\,⟹\,x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

And substituting $c=-1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
-10(-1)y=-5\,⟹\,y=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $y=-\frac{1}{2}$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =4-2{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-5{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =4-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{5}{4} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2},\frac{9}{4}).$

Question 5
?

At which point on the surface z=4−2x2−5y2 is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector v=⟨−2,−5,1⟩?

a
(12,1,−32)
b
(−1,1,−3)
c
(−12,−12,94)
d
(2,−1,−9)
e
(1,0,2)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface z=f(x,y) at the point (x0,y0,z0) on the surface can be written as z−z0=(x−x0)∂f∂x(x0,y0)+(y−y0)∂f∂y(x0,y0), where ⟨∂f∂x(x0,y0),∂f∂y(x0,y0),−1⟩ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives: ∂f∂x=∂∂x(4−2x2−5y2)=−4x∂f∂y=∂∂y(4−2x2−5y2)=−10y

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is ⟨−4x,−10y,−1⟩.

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to ⟨−2,−5,1⟩. So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant c, we must have c⋅⟨−4x,−10y,−1⟩=⟨−2,−5,1⟩.

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system: {−4cx=−2−10cy=−5−c=1

From the third equation, we get c=−1. Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain −4(−1)x=−2⟹x=−12.

And substituting c=−1 into the second equation, we have −10(−1)y=−5⟹y=−12.

Finally, substituting x=−12 and y=−12 into our function, we get z=4−2(−12)2−5(−12)2=4−12−54=94.

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector v at (−12,−12,94).

solution.reasoning: A normal to the tangent plane is (4x,10y,1). It must be parallel to (−2,−5,1); the third components force the proportionality factor to be 1. Hence x=−1/2 and y=−1/2, giving z=4−1/2−5/4=9/4. Option c is mathematically correct. No Math Academy answer-key evidence was provided.

feedback.problem: At which point on the surface $z=4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2}$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector $v=⟨-2,-5,1⟩?$
feedback.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2})=-4x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(4-2{x}^{2}-5{y}^{2})=-10y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨-2,-5,1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨-4x,\,-10y,\,-1⟩=⟨-2,-5,1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}-4cx=-2 \\ -10cy=-5 \\ -c=1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
-4(-1)x=-2\,⟹\,x=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

And substituting $c=-1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
-10(-1)y=-5\,⟹\,y=-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=-\frac{1}{2}$ and $y=-\frac{1}{2}$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =4-2{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}-5{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2} \\  & =4-\frac{1}{2}-\frac{5}{4} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(-\frac{1}{2},-\frac{1}{2},\frac{9}{4}).$

questions.name: Question 1
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with normal vector $\overset{~}{n},$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨y,\,x-z,\,-2x⟩\,,\,\overset{~}{n}(x,y,z)=⟨2x,\,-z,\,y⟩\,,\,n=\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖}.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}\frac{\boxed{}}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S
$$

what is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

To compute the above dot product, we must normalize the vector $\overset{~}{n}.$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨2x,\,-z,\,y⟩}{\sqrt{(2x)^{2}+(-z)^{2}+(y)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨2x,\,-z,\,y⟩}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{z}^{2}+{y}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨2x,\,-z,\,y⟩}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$

$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\,\frac{{z}^{2}-xz}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 2
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨xy,\,yz,\,xz⟩\,,\,n(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,-1,\,2⟩\,.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S=\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{∬}_{S}\boxed{}\,\text{d}S,
$$

what is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨xy,\,yz,\,xz⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨1,\,-1,\,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}⟨xy,\,yz,\,xz⟩\cdot ⟨1,\,-1,\,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}(xy-yz+2xz) \\  & =\frac{xy-yz+2xz}{\sqrt{6}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{xy-yz+2xz}{\sqrt{6}}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}{∬}_{S}xy-yz+2xz\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 3
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with normal vector $\overset{~}{n},$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩\,,\,\overset{~}{n}(x,y,z)=⟨2y,\,-z,\,2x⟩\,,\,n=\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖}.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}\frac{\boxed{}}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S
$$

what is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

To compute the above dot product, we must normalize the vector $\overset{~}{n}.$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨2y,\,-z,\,2x⟩}{\sqrt{(2y)^{2}+(-z)^{2}+(2x)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨2y,\,-z,\,2x⟩}{\sqrt{4{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+4{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨2y,\,-z,\,2x⟩}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot \frac{⟨2y,\,-z,\,2x⟩}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot ⟨2y,\,-z,\,2x⟩}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2yz-yz+2{x}^{2}}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2{x}^{2}+yz}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\,\frac{2{x}^{2}+yz}{\sqrt{4{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 4
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with unit normal vector $n,$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨\frac{z}{2},\,x,\,z-y⟩\,,\,n(x,y,z)=\frac{1}{5}⟨4,\,0,\,-3⟩\,.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S=\frac{1}{5}{∬}_{S}\boxed{}\,\text{d}S,
$$

what is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨\frac{z}{2},\,x,\,z-y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{5}⟨4,\,0,\,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}⟨\frac{z}{2},\,x,\,z-y⟩\cdot ⟨4,\,0,\,-3⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{5}(2z+0-3(z-y)) \\  & =\frac{3y-z}{5}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{3y-z}{5}\,\text{d}S \\  & =\frac{1}{5}{∬}_{S}3y-z\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 5
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F$ and the surface $S$ with normal vector $\overset{~}{n},$ where

$$
F(x,y,z)=⟨{x}^{2},\,2xz,\,x+y⟩\,,\,\overset{~}{n}(x,y,z)=⟨-3z,\,x,\,2y⟩\,,\,n=\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖}.
$$

If the flux of $F$ across $S$ with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}\frac{2xy+2{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}z}{\boxed{}}\,\text{d}S
$$

what is the missing expression?
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

To compute the above dot product, we must normalize the vector $\overset{~}{n}.$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-3z,\,x,\,2y⟩}{\sqrt{(-3z)^{2}+(x)^{2}+(2y)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨-3z,\,x,\,2y⟩}{\sqrt{9{z}^{2}+{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨-3z,\,x,\,2y⟩}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+9{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨{x}^{2},\,2xz,\,x+y⟩\cdot \frac{⟨-3z,\,x,\,2y⟩}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+9{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨{x}^{2},\,2xz,\,x+y⟩\cdot ⟨-3z,\,x,\,2y⟩}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+9{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{-3{x}^{2}z+2{x}^{2}z+2y(x+y)}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+9{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2xy+2{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+9{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\,\frac{2xy+2{y}^{2}-{x}^{2}z}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}+9{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 6
questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨4y,\,5x,\,2z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=3$ for $1\le x\le 2$ and $1\le y\le 3.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=3$ for  $1\le x\le 2$ and $1\le y\le 3,$ the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=3$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨4y,\,5x,\,2z⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨4y,\,5x,\,6⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}6\,\text{d}S \\  & =6{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =6{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =6{\int }_{1}^{3}\text{d}y{\int }_{1}^{2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =6\cdot (3-1)\cdot (2-1) \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 7
questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,x,\,3x+y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=-1$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $1\le y\le 2.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is a continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=-1$ for  $0\le x\le 2$ and $1\le y\le 2,$ the downward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=-1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,x,\,3x+y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-(3x+y).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(-(3x+y))\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-(3x+y))\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2}(-(3x+y))\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{1}^{2}[(\frac{3}{2}{x}^{2}+xy){|}_{x=0}^{x=2}\,]\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{1}^{2}(6+2y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{[6y+{y}^{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =-9\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 8
questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨y,\,z,\,2x⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 2.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 2,$ the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨y,\,z,\,2x⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨y,\,2,\,2x⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =2x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}2x\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{3}2x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{3}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =2\cdot {[{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{3} \\  & =18\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 9
questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,y-x,\,x+y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=2$ for  $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1,$ the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=2$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,y-x,\,x+y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨2,\,y-x,\,x+y⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =x+y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(x+y)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(x+y)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}+xy]}_{x=0}^{x=1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\frac{1}{2}+y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}\,y+\frac{1}{2}\,{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 10
questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=1$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=1$ for  $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1,$ the upward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
n=⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩.
$$

Using the fact that $z=1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,1⟩ \\  & =x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}x\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\text{d}x \\  & =1\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 11
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=x+y$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $0\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\sqrt{3}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x+y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+(-1)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x+y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}⟨x+y,\,y,\,x⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,-1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-(x+y)-y+x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}(-2y) \\  & =-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\,y)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}y\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-\frac{2}{\cancel{\sqrt{3}}}y\cdot \cancel{\sqrt{3}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-2y\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}-2y\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-[{y}^{2}]_{0}^{1}\cdot [x]_{0}^{3} \\  & =-1\cdot 3 \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 12
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x,\,z,\,y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=\frac{1}{2}x-y-1$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 3.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\frac{3}{2}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=\frac{1}{2}x-y-1$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-\frac{1}{2},\,1,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=-1,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨\frac{1}{2},\,-1,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=1.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨-\frac{1}{2},\,1,\,1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-\frac{1}{2},\,1,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}⟨-\frac{1}{2},\,1,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-1,\,2,\,2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=\frac{1}{2}x-y-1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,z,\,y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-1,\,2,\,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x,\,\frac{1}{2}x-y-1,\,y⟩\cdot ⟨-1,\,2,\,2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-x+(x-2y-2)+2y) \\  & =-\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(-\frac{2}{3})\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\frac{2}{3})\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\frac{2}{3})\cdot \frac{3}{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-\frac{\cancel{2}}{\cancel{3}})\cdot \frac{\cancel{3}}{\cancel{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-1\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =-3\cdot 1 \\  & =-3\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 13
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2x+2y-2$ for $0\le x\le 3$ and $-1\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=3.$*
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=2x+2y-2$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=-2,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=2.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=2x+2y-2$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x,\,y,\,2x+2y-2⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2x+2y-(2x+2y-2)) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{2}{3}\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{3}\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{3}\cdot 3\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{\cancel{3}}\cdot \cancel{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2\,\text{d}A \\  & =2{\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{3}\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{-1}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & =2\cdot 3\cdot 2 \\  & =12\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 14
questions.problem:
Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨x,\,2y,\,2z-x-y⟩$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=x-\frac{y}{2}+3$ for $0\le x\le 2$ and $-1\le y\le 1.$ Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||=\frac{3}{2}.$*
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=x-\frac{y}{2}+3$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-1,\,\frac{1}{2},\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=3,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨1,\,-\frac{1}{2},\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=-3.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨1,\,-\frac{1}{2},\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨1,\,-\frac{1}{2},\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{1}^{2}+{(-\frac{1}{2})}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{2}{3}⟨1,\,-\frac{1}{2},\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,-1,\,-2⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=x-\frac{y}{2}+3$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,2y,\,2z-x-y⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,-1,\,-2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x,\,2y,\,(2x-y+6)-x-y⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,-1,\,-2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨x,\,2y,\,x-2y+6⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,-1,\,-2⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2x-2y-2(x-2y+6)) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2y-12).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{1}{3}(2y-12)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{3}(2y-12)\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{3}(2y-12)\cdot \frac{3}{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{\cancel{3}}(2y-12)\cdot \frac{\cancel{3}}{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(y-6)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{1}(y-6)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}x\cdot {\int }_{-1}^{1}(y-6)\,\text{d}y \\  & =[x]_{0}^{2}\cdot {[\frac{{y}^{2}}{2}-6y]}_{-1}^{1} \\  & =2\cdot (-12) \\  & =-24\end{aligned}
$$

questions.name: Question 15
questions.problem: Consider the vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨3-x,\,x+y,\,z-2x⟩$ and a finite region $S$ of the plane $z=2x+2y$ such that $\text{Area}(S)=3.$  Calculate the flux of $F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $n.$
questions.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $n,$ and $F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $n$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z=2x+2y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩}_{⏟}}_{\overset{~}{n}}=0,\,\text{or}\,⟨x,\,y,\,z⟩\cdot {{⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩}_{⏟}}_{-\overset{~}{n}}=0.
$$

Since we require a downward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is negative. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\overset{~}{n}=⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩}{\sqrt{{2}^{2}+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=2x+2y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨3-x,\,x+y,\,z-2x⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨3-x,\,x+y,\,2y⟩\cdot ⟨2,\,2,\,-1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2(3-x)+2(x+y)-2y) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(6-2x+2x+2y-2y) \\  & =\frac{6}{3} \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}2\,\text{d}S \\  & =2{∬}_{S}\,\text{d}S \\  & =2\cdot \text{Area}(S) \\  & =2\cdot 3 \\  & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Rewriting a Flux Integral as a Surface Integral
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf F$ and the surface $S$ with normal vector $\widetilde{\mathbf n},$ where

$$
\mathbf{F}(x,y,z) = \left\langle x,\: 2z,\: z-y \right\rangle\!, 
\quad 
\widetilde{\mathbf{n}}(x,y,z) = \left\langle z,\: -y,\: -x \right\rangle\!,
\quad
\mathbf n = \dfrac{\widetilde{\mathbf{n}}}{\Vert \widetilde{\mathbf{n}} \Vert}.
$$

If the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ with respect to $\mathbf{n}$ is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224379/assets/4152d997be216db1a67b5f55ee112d1008ea7399e57f699ac62ba03654bd7fd5.svg)

what is the missing expression?
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

To compute the above dot product, we must normalize the vector $\widetilde{\mathbf n}.$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨z,\,-y,\,-x⟩}{\sqrt{(z)^{2}+(-y)^{2}+(-x)^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨z,\,-y,\,-x⟩}{\sqrt{{z}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{x}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨z,\,-y,\,-x⟩}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Calculating the dot product, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨x,\,2z,\,z-y⟩\cdot \frac{⟨z,\,-y,\,-x⟩}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{⟨x,\,2z,\,z-y⟩\cdot ⟨z,\,-y,\,-x⟩}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{xz-2yz-x(z-y)}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{xy-2yz}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the flux can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\,\frac{xy-2yz}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}}}\,\text{d}S.\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Rewriting a Flux Integral as a Surface Integral

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Horizontal Plane
canonical_examples.problem: Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle z,\: z,\: 4xy\rangle$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=1$ for $0\leq x\leq 1$ and $0\leq y\leq 1.$ Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ with respect to the *downward*-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

For the surface $z=1$ for  $0\leq x\leq 1$ and $0\leq y\leq 1,$ the downward-pointing unit normal vector is

$$
\mathbf n = \langle 0,\, 0,\, -1\rangle.
$$

Using the fact that $z=1$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨z,\,z,\,4xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,1,\,4xy⟩\cdot ⟨0,\,0,\,-1⟩ \\  & =-4xy.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}(-4xy)\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-4xy)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(-4xy)\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{1}2y\,\text{d}y{\int }_{0}^{1}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =-{[{y}^{2}]}_{0}^{1}\cdot {[{x}^{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Horizontal Plane

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane
canonical_examples.problem:
Consider the vector field $\mathbf F(x,y,z) = \langle y,\: 0,\: z\rangle$ and the surface $S$ defined in Cartesian coordinates as $z=2x+2y$ for $0\leq x\leq 2$ and $0\leq y\leq 1.$ Calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ through $S$ with respect to the upward-pointing unit normal vector $\mathbf n.$

*Hint: You're given that the fundamental vector product of $S$ with respect to its canonical parametrization is $||\mathbf r_x \times \mathbf r_y|| =3.$*
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
If $S$ is an oriented surface with unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and $\mathbf F$ is continuous vector field, then the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ measured with respect to $\mathbf n$ is given by

$$
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \textrm{d}\mathbf{S}
=
\iint\limits_S \mathbf{F} \cdot \mathbf{n} \,\textrm{d}S.
$$

Notice that our surface $z = 2x+2y$ can be written using the dot product as 

$$
\langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle -2,\: -2, \: 1\rangle}_{\widetilde{\mathbf n}} = 0, \quad \textrm{or}\quad \langle x,\: y,\: z\rangle \cdot \underbrace{\langle 2,\: 2, \: -1\rangle}_{-\widetilde{\mathbf n}}= 0.
$$

Since we require an upward-pointing normal vector to our surface $S,$ we must select one where the $z$-component is positive. This gives us the normal vector

$$
\widetilde{\mathbf n} = \langle -2,\, -2,\, 1\rangle.
$$

Normalizing this vector, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}n & =\frac{\overset{~}{n}}{‖\overset{~}{n}‖} \\  & =\frac{⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩}{\sqrt{(-2)^{2}+(-2)^{2}+{1}^{2}}} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Using the fact that $z=2x+2y$ on $S,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}F\cdot n & =⟨y,\,0,\,z⟩\cdot \frac{1}{3}⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}⟨y,\,0,\,2x+2y⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,-2,\,1⟩ \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(-2y+0x+2x+2y) \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(2x) \\  & =\frac{2}{3}x.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the flux of $\mathbf F$ across $S$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{S}\frac{2}{3}x\,\text{d}S \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{3}x\cdot ||{r}_{x}\times {r}_{y}||\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{3}x\cdot 3\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{2}{\cancel{3}}x\cdot \cancel{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2x\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y\cdot {\int }_{0}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =[y]_{0}^{1}\cdot [{x}^{2}]_{0}^{2} \\  & =1\cdot 4 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$
canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Computing the Flux of a Vector Field Through a Tilted Plane

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Recall that the flux of a two-dimensional vector field $\mathbf F(x,y)$ across a curve $C$ with respect to a unit normal vector $\mathbf n(x,y)$ is given by the line integral

$$
\int\limits_C \mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,\textrm d s.
$$

The flux measures the total flow of $\mathbf F$ through $C,$ as depicted below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224379/assets/2392d6c27fc6767c78172936d6df37b3dfec8b2198abbdf9e22b87d4337ed9da.png)

Flux is always measured with respect to a preselected unit normal vector $\mathbf n,$ and we have two choices of orientation for this vector. If we measure the flux relative to the unit normal pointing in the *opposite* direction, our flux will have the *same* magnitude but *opposite* sign.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224379/assets/e451548a5d9874b9eff9d61c2d423696dc76a3f560e2936eb7bdb3a9cbfbed49.png)

This lesson aims to extend the concept of flux to three-dimensional vector fields. But first, we need a brief discussion on surface orientations.

tutorials.name: Orientable vs. Non-Orientable Surfaces
tutorials.problem:
A surface is **orientable** if it has two distinct sides. So, for example, the surface $S$ shown below is orientable.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224379/assets/29be1e415eaf0072aea7f4093e71665f5996b29804702a37a4d4493e0b0002d4.png)

 

If a unit vector $\mathbf n(x,y,z)$ to our orientable surface varies continuously over $S,$ we say that $S$ is **oriented** and the choice of $\mathbf n$ gives an **orientation** of $S.$

We can choose the opposite orientation for our surface by selecting a vector that points in the opposite direction, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224379/assets/40268c448b7c4ac99acf356e9f1e2702112a0d46dc1b6e6afd98d5c95e5ea317.png)

 

When dealing with two-sided (i.e., orientable) surfaces, we must always be clear about our chosen orientation. 

Note that some surfaces are *not* orientable. This means they do not have two distinct sides. An example of a non-orientable surface is a Möbius strip, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14224379/assets/277ffb9e1594e64f3411b0c5063841616aaa433ccc4915bc96e2c9ab865ece95.png)

 

A Möbius strip can be made by taking a long rectangular piece of paper, twisting one of its ends by $180^\circ$ and gluing the two ends together. 

A Möbius strip does not have two distinct sides because if you were to start at a point $P$ on the strip and move along it (following the dark blue curve shown), you'd eventually end up at the same point but on the opposite side! Thus, a Möbius strip only has one distinct side. 

In the work that follows, we will only consider orientable surfaces.
